L259: ## What it measures
L260: 
L261: Per concurrency level it reports successful operations/sec, p50/p95/p99/p99.9/max latency, and CAS-failure / error counts where they apply. Results print as a table and are written to `results/forgemark-<id>.json` for charting.
L262: ### Strategies
L263: `-strategy`  | shape  | what it tells you
L264: --- | --- | ---
L265: `branch` (default)  | N agents, one repo, each pushes its own branch  | Headline single-repo number. No client-side contention (each agent owns its ref), so it isolates the server's per-repo ref-update path.
L266: `repo`  | N agents spread across M repos (`-repo-count`), own branches  | Horizontal-scale ceiling — distinct repos serialize independently, so this should scale where `branch` saturates.
L267: `clone`  | N agents, one repo, each loops: shallow-clone the base branch → discard → repeat  | Read-side ceiling: how many concurrent shallow clones/sec the forge sustains, without write load.
L268: `session`  | N agents, each loops: shallow-clone the base branch → commit+push `-session-commits` checkpoints to a fresh ephemeral branch → abandon → repeat  | Realistic agent lifecycle: interleaves read load (clone) with write load (push) on one repo. Reports clone and push latencies separately.
L269: ## Usage
L270: 
L271: Two steps: set up the target repos, then run.
L272: ### 1. Set up targets
L273: 
L274: ForgeMark does not create repos — it pushes to ones you provide. Create them on your forge and make sure your credential can push:
L275: 
L276:   * `branch` needs one empty repo.
L277:   * `repo` needs M empty repos.
L278:   * `clone` and `session` need a repo with a base branch that has content to clone. An empty repo degrades to a no-read orphan, so a read-side run against an unseeded repo isn't measuring what you think — push a base branch first.
L279: Per forge, roughly:
L280: 
L281:     # GitHub (needs the gh CLI): a throwaway private repo
L282:     gh repo create you/forgemark-target --private
L283:     # for clone/session runs, give it content:
L284:     #   git clone … && git commit --allow-empty -m base && git push
L285: 
L286:     # GitLab (needs the glab CLI): a throwaway private project
L287:     glab repo create forgemark-target --private
L288: 
L289:     # Gitea / self-hosted: create an empty repo in the UI or via the forge's API,
L290:     # ensure your token/user can push, and (for clone/session) push a base branch
L291:     # with at least one commit.
L292: 
L293:     # Entire, native EntireDB repo (needs the entire CLI): repos live on ONE
L294:     # cluster, so point the target's remote at that cluster's URL. Repo path:
L295:     # et/forgemark-<you>/forgemark-target
L296:     entire project create forgemark-<you> --owner github:<you> --owner-type account --region <region>
L297:     entire repo create forgemark-target --project forgemark-<you> --cluster-host <cluster>
L298: 
L299:     # Entire, GitHub mirror (write-throughs to GitHub on every push — benchmarks
L300:     # the sync flow, not the forge alone). Repo path: gh/<you>/forgemark-target
L301:     entire repo mirror create https://github.com/<you>/forgemark-target <cluster>
L302: ### 2. Run
L303: Most forges just need a token. Point `-remote` at the host and supply the token via `-token-file` (a file, or `-` for stdin):
L304: 
L305:     FORGE="-remote https://git.example.com"
L306: 
L307:     # Headline: single-repo throughput, sweep concurrency
L308:     # (-token-file reads a file; use "-" to pipe the token in on stdin instead)
L309:     forgemark $FORGE -token-file ~/.forge-token \
L310:       -repos org/repo -concurrency 1,8,32 -duration 2m
L311: 
L312:     # Spread across 16 repos (horizontal scale)
L313:     forgemark $FORGE -token-file ~/.forge-token -strategy repo \
L314:       -repo-pattern "org/bench-{n}" -repo-count 16 -concurrency 32,128 -duration 2m
L315: 
L316:     # Clone: read-side throughput, discard each in-memory clone (needs a seeded base branch)
L317:     forgemark $FORGE -token-file ~/.forge-token -repos org/repo \
L318:       -strategy clone -clone-depth 1 -concurrency 8,32 -duration 2m
L319: 
L320:     # Session: clone + push 5 checkpoints, abandon, repeat (needs a seeded base branch)
L321:     forgemark $FORGE -token-file ~/.forge-token -repos org/repo \
L322:       -strategy session -session-commits 5 -clone-depth 1 -concurrency 8,32
L323: The push URL is `<-remote>/<repo>` — the `-repos` value is appended verbatim (ForgeMark does no path rewriting), so include a `.git` suffix if your forge needs it. The token is used as the basic-auth password with a conventional username (`-user` to override); most forges accept a PAT this way. The secret comes from `-token-file` or the `ACCESS_TOKEN` env var — never a CLI flag, so it can't leak via `ps` or shell history. Entire needs a couple of extra flags — see below.
L324: ## Entire
L325: Entire needs two extra flags — `-token-url` and `-jurisdiction`; their presence selects the Entire path. Auth is your account access token, presented directly: entiredb authorizes every push live, so one token covers every repo you can reach. Pass it as `-token-file`/`ACCESS_TOKEN`:
L326: 
L327:     forgemark -remote https://aws-us-east-2.entire.io \
L328:       -token-url    https://us.auth.entire.io/oauth/token \
L329:       -jurisdiction https://us.entire.io \
L330:       -token-file   ~/.entire-subject-token \
L331:       -repos your/repo -concurrency 1,8,32,128 -duration 2m
L332: `-repos` is appended verbatim — ForgeMark does no path rewriting, so pass the full repo path exactly as your Entire deployment expects it. The exact form is deployment-specific — see the runbook.
L333: 
L334: Deployment-specific setup (obtaining the subject token, target provisioning) and methodology notes live in Entire's own runbook.
L335: ## github.com
L336: 
L337: github.com is just a generic remote — point `-remote` at it with a PAT (needs contents: write):
L338: 
L339:     gh repo create you/forgemark-throwaway --private
L340:     gh auth token | forgemark -remote https://github.com -token-file - \
L341:       -repos you/forgemark-throwaway -concurrency 1,4 -duration 30s
L342: Keep concurrency low. github.com applies secondary rate limits and abuse detection to high-volume content writes; a tight push loop at high concurrency will get throttled or blocked, and high-volume automated load testing of github.com isn't sanctioned by their acceptable-use policy. ForgeMark detects a `github.com` remote and warns above concurrency 16. For a higher-volume comparison, point `-remote` at a GitHub Enterprise Server you control.
L343: ## GitLab
L344: GitLab is also a generic remote. The push path wants a repository-scoped credential, which is not always what `glab auth token` returns — so pull the credential from glab's git-credential helper (username `oauth2`, password a repo-scoped token):
L345: 
L346:     glab repo create forgemark-target --private
L347:     CRED=$(printf 'protocol=https\nhost=gitlab.com\n\n' | glab auth git-credential get)
L348:     printf '%s' "$CRED" | sed -n 's/^password=//p' \
L349:       | forgemark -remote https://gitlab.com -token-file - -user oauth2 \
L350:           -repos you/forgemark-target.git -concurrency 1,8 -duration 1m
L351: The web GUI does this for you: pick glab CLI login as the credential source (or Add from CLI logins) and the server runs the helper at run start. As with github.com, gitlab.com rate-limits high-volume writes — keep concurrency modest, or point `-remote` at a self-managed GitLab you control.
L352: ## Key flags
L353: flag  | default  | notes
L354: --- | --- | ---
L355: `-remote`  | —  | base URL of the forge (e.g. `https://gitlab.com`); the cluster base URL for Entire
L356: `-token-file`  | —  | file holding the credential secret; `-` reads stdin (else `$ACCESS_TOKEN`)
L357: `-user`  | `x-access-token`  | basic-auth username (token forges ignore it)
L358: `-repos` / `-repo-pattern`+`-repo-count`  | —  | target repo path(s), appended verbatim; `-repo-pattern` expands `{n}` to `1..N`
L359: `-strategy`  | `branch`  | `branch` | `repo` | `clone` | `session`
L360: `-ref-namespace`  | `refs/forgemark/`  | where pushed refs land; the default stays off `refs/heads/` so the forge's post-receive pipeline (search ingestion, CI, webhooks) never sees bench pushes. `refs/heads/` pushes real branches
L361: `-branch-prefix`  | —  | prepended verbatim inside the namespace, before the run ID (e.g. `bench/` → `refs/forgemark/bench/fm...`); groups refs for easy cleanup
L362: `-push-options`  | —  | push option sent with every push, like `git push -o` (e.g. `ci.skip`); repeat the flag for several. The run refuses to start unless every repo advertises the `push-options` capability, since go-git would otherwise drop them silently
L363: `-concurrency`  | `1,8,32,128`  | swept sequentially, one row each
L364: `-duration` / `-warmup`  | `60s` / `10s`  | measured window / discarded ramp
L365: `-files-min`/`-files-max`/`-file-size`  | `1`/`10`/`2048`  | commit shape; ignored by `clone`
L366: `-object-format`  | `auto`  | `sha1` | `sha256`; `auto` probes the Entire advertisement (generic/github default sha1)
L367: `-session-commits`  | `5`  | session strategy checkpoints per cloned session
L368: `-clone-depth`/`-base-ref`  | `1`/default  | clone/session strategy knobs
L369: `-insecure`  | `false`  | skip TLS verification (dev / self-signed hosts)
L370: `-out`  | —  | JSON results path (default `results/forgemark-<id>.json`)
L371: ### Entire (supplying `-token-url` + `-jurisdiction` selects it)
L372: 
L373: flag  | notes
L374: --- | ---
L375: `-token-url`  | core `/oauth/token` endpoint (presence selects Entire; not dialed)
L376: `-jurisdiction`  | jurisdiction host, bare origin (presence selects Entire)
L377: `-client-id`  | accepted for compatibility; unused
L378: 
L379: In this mode `-token-file`/`ACCESS_TOKEN` carries the account access token, not a forge PAT.
L380: ## Environment variables
L381: 
L382: var  | notes
L383: --- | ---
L384: `ACCESS_TOKEN`  | the credential secret, if `-token-file` isn't given: the forge token, or Entire's subject token. `-token-file` is preferred (keeps the secret out of the environment too).
L385: ## How it works
L386:   * Each agent keeps an in-memory go-git repo (object format matched to the remote), commits 1–10 small files per iteration, and pushes its own ref in a tight loop. Agents are pinned round-robin across the target's nodes.
L387:   * Pushed refs land under `refs/forgemark/` (see `-ref-namespace`), not `refs/heads/`. Receive-pack does the same work for any ref — packfile unpack, connectivity check, ref update — so the measured latency is the same, but a branch would also trigger whatever the forge runs post-receive (search ingestion, CI, webhooks), which is paid-for, rate-limited work on the target and never shows up in the number anyway. Pass `-ref-namespace refs/heads/` to load that pipeline on purpose.
L388:   * Clone runs create each shallow clone in memory and discard it after recording latency, so the client side stays off disk.
L389:   * Stats: every operation is timed; warm-up samples are dropped; exact percentiles are computed from the sorted OK-latency set.
L390: ## Caveats
L391:   * Run the generator close to the target (same region). Push latency from a distant machine is dominated by round-trip time, so you'd be measuring the network path, not the forge. Watch the generator's CPU stays below 100% at the top concurrency level, or it — not the server — is your bottleneck.
L392:   * `branch`/`repo` leave one per-agent ref each on the target (swept by the next run once they're a week old — including leftovers under `refs/heads/` from forgemark versions that predate `-ref-namespace`); `session` deletes each ephemeral ref as the agent abandons it; `clone` does not write refs. Use throwaway repos regardless. Pass `-branch-prefix` (e.g. `bench/`) to group the refs so they're easy to find and delete on the target afterwards.

# Agents

> Configure automated Trail evaluations and write custom agents for your repository.

## What Are Agents?

Agents are configurable AI jobs that review changes in a Trail and evaluate them using customizable instructions. They run in isolated cloud sandboxes and can produce summaries, identify code review findings, or report evaluation scores.
Agents can evaluate different aspects of a change, such as Confidence, Risk, Security, and Drift. Each Agent can report a score and flag issues that need attention as Findings.
[Gates](https://docs.entire.com/guides/trails/gates.md) define the requirements that determine whether a Trail can merge. Once configured, your Agents will look something like this:

![Trail change showing code review, security review, Slop, and monitor results](https://mintcdn.com/entire/7Crxbl28PbL5RtNq/images/trails-agent-evaluations.png?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=7Crxbl28PbL5RtNq\&q=85\&s=4610de86a7092c06ee944efba8aa4ad5)

Agent evaluation results on a Trail change.

## How Agents Work

With Agents and Auto build on push enabled in repository settings, pushing changes to a Trail branch triggers the configured Agents. Each Agent uses its instructions and selected configuration to evaluate the changes.
Entire displays the results on the Trail. Reviewers can use the scores to focus their review, investigate Findings, and push fixes for another evaluation.
The available preset Agents include:

* **Code review:** Reviews every push and flags what needs to be fixed.
* **Security review:** Checks every change for anything that could lead to a security breach in your codebase.
* **Slop:** Catches sloppy patterns and drift before you merge them on your main codebase.

![Entire agent presets for code review, security review, and detecting sloppy patterns and drift](https://mintcdn.com/entire/7Crxbl28PbL5RtNq/images/trails-agent-presets.png?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=7Crxbl28PbL5RtNq\&q=85\&s=93c0acfa9a7304c2ba1d23c2e9814313)

Preset agents available on the project's Agents page.

The default monitor scores range from 0 to 100. You can read their rationale alongside the score and the underlying code. Here’s an example of how it looks:

![Security score dialog showing a score of 5 percent, supporting rationale, and evaluation history](https://mintcdn.com/entire/7Crxbl28PbL5RtNq/images/trails-security-score-rationale.png?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=7Crxbl28PbL5RtNq\&q=85\&s=7d4f9ca58baad806be05037e7b371482)

A Security monitor score with its rationale and history.

## Set Up Your First Agent

To create your first Agent:

1. Navigate to your project on Entire.com.
2. Open your project and go to **Agents** then click on **Manage Agents**.

[Open project Agents](https://customer-0x5hsk8lh27fm00g.cloudflarestream.com/e24c2efca1b9ae12221bcd13cf14b677/iframe)

3. Choose an Agent from the list of presets and click **Enable** to start using it.

[Enable a preset agent](https://customer-0x5hsk8lh27fm00g.cloudflarestream.com/87c891fe2bf2042b7c4e1b12c7e19248/iframe)

## Creating a Custom Agent

If you want to create an Agent with your own configuration, follow these steps:

Click **New agent**. Under Agent, give it a name and description. Select the harness, model, reasoning effort, and timeout. Then write the Instructions describing what the Agent should review and evaluate.
For example, you can create a Migration Risk Agent to evaluate database migration changes.
Under **Agent**, enter the following details:

* Name: Migration Risk
* Description: Evaluates database migration changes for potential deployment and rollback risks.
* Harness, model, reasoning effort, and timeout: Select the configuration that meets your evaluation requirements.

Instructions:

```text theme={null}
Evaluate database migration risk in the Trail's changes. Inspect changed migrations and related application code for destructive operations, locking, compatibility during rollout, and rollback safety.
Score risk from 0 to 100, where higher values indicate greater potential damage. If no migration-related changes exist, return 0 and explain why.
Provide a short rationale explaining the evidence behind the score.
```

Configure the signal the Agent reports by selecting its value type and polarity. The value type determines how the score is represented, while the polarity determines whether higher or lower values are better.

Under **Trigger**, choose when the Agent runs. You can select Trail branch pushed, Run manually, or Recurring schedule.

Under **Repositories**, select at least one repository where the Agent should run.

[Create a custom agent](https://customer-0x5hsk8lh27fm00g.cloudflarestream.com/54a12ce490642658eceaddaa1a963784/iframe)

Leave the **Active** toggle enabled and click **Create agent**.
After it is successfully created, you should see it under the Agents tab as in the image below.

![Agents page listing an active Payments reviewer with its repositories and selected model](https://mintcdn.com/entire/7Crxbl28PbL5RtNq/images/trails-custom-agent.png?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=7Crxbl28PbL5RtNq\&q=85\&s=b5305477d17ae14bdf06b753c67850bc)

A custom agent listed on the project’s Agents page.

Once configured, the Agent can evaluate changes, report a score, and flag issues as Findings.

## Understand the Agent Configuration

| Setting | Purpose |
| - | - |
| Name and description | Identify the Agent and describe what it evaluates. |
| Harness | Select the coding agent environment used for evaluation. |
| Model | Choose the AI model used by the Agent. |
| Reasoning effort | Configure how much reasoning the model uses during evaluation. |
| Timeout | Set the maximum time allowed for an evaluation. |
| Instructions | Define what the Agent should review and how it should evaluate changes. |
| Value type | Define how the Agent's evaluation score is represented. |
| Polarity | Specify whether higher or lower scores indicate a better result. |
| Trigger | Choose when the Agent runs: on Trail branch pushes, manually, or on a recurring schedule. |
| Repositories | Select the repositories where the Agent runs. |
| Active | Enable or disable the Agent. |

## Agent Insights

Agent Insights helps you understand how coding agents use tokens across your Trails and repositories. You can track token consumption by activity, compare usage across models, and identify changes that required more agent effort than expected.

### How to Enable Agent Insights

To start tracking agent token usage, go to the Plugins tab in your project and find the Agent Insights extension.
Click Install, select the repositories on Entire where you want to enable Agent Insights, and click Install again.

[Install Agent Insights](https://customer-0x5hsk8lh27fm00g.cloudflarestream.com/0445a8cbe2442fc3528bde0ce38fcc3e/iframe)

### View Token Usage in a Trail

Once it is enabled, open a Trail and navigate to Sessions to see a breakdown of token usage across agent activities, such as understanding code, building, checking, reworking, reviewing, and coordinating.
Hover over the visualization to see the percentage of tokens spent on each activity. This helps you understand how the agent worked on a change and whether it spent more tokens implementing changes or making repeated fixes.

![Sessions token usage bar with a tooltip showing percentages for understanding, building, checking, reworking, shipping, coordinating, and reviewing](https://mintcdn.com/entire/7Crxbl28PbL5RtNq/images/trails-agent-insights-activities.png?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=7Crxbl28PbL5RtNq\&q=85\&s=6554d6bb00f76b360bd9249e07058710)

Token usage by activity within a Trail’s Sessions section.

### View Agent Insights in Repository Analytics

Open your repository's existing Analytics page and scroll to the Agent Insights section.
The Analytics page is available independently of the plugin. Enabling Agent Insights adds more detailed token usage metrics across merged Trails through three visualizations:

* **Token Volume by Model:** Track daily token consumption grouped by the models used.
* **Tokens vs. Lines Changed:** Compare token usage against the number of lines modified in each Trail. This helps identify which Trails consume the most tokens.
* **Tokens by Activity:** Compare token usage across activities between the current and previous week to understand how agent behavior changes over time.

You can use these metrics to identify unusual token consumption, understand which activities require the most effort, and compare agent usage across Trails.

![Repository charts for token volume by model, tokens versus lines changed, and tokens by activity](https://mintcdn.com/entire/7Crxbl28PbL5RtNq/images/trails-agent-insights-analytics.png?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=7Crxbl28PbL5RtNq\&q=85\&s=675840a06ebde8695b6d9af717f3e905)

Agent Insights on the repository Analytics page.

> Use this file to discover all available pages before exploring further.

# Gates

> Configure the requirements a Trail must satisfy before it can merge.

## What Are Gates?

Gates are merge requirements for a Trail. They bring branch freshness, human review, agent findings, and CI checks into one place so your team can see what is satisfied, pending, or blocking a merge.

While [Agents](https://docs.entire.com/guides/trails/agents.md) produce automated evaluations, Gates apply your repository's merge policy to the relevant evidence, including unresolved review findings and check results.

## Configure Gates

With repository admin permission:

1. Open your repository in entire.com.
2. Select **Settings** then **Gates**.
3. Turn on **Enable gates**.
4. Enable the Gates that you need for your repository.
5. Configure the requirements for each enabled gate.
6. Choose who may bypass a blocking gate.

Start with the requirements your team already uses for pull requests. Set up and merge the `trail-review` runner before making **Agent review** blocking.

[Configure Gates](https://customer-0x5hsk8lh27fm00g.cloudflarestream.com/fa86858d668db71f2eab5aed5b29fb35/iframe)

### Up to Date

This gate checks whether the Trail's branch is current with its base branch. You need to configure whether to allow a clean merge when the branch is behind. Use a blocking requirement when your team needs changes evaluated against the latest base before merging.

### Human Review

This gate evaluates approvals submitted on the Trail. Configure:

* The minimum number of approvals.
* Whether the Trail author's approval counts.
* Whether new pushes reset existing approvals.

For example, require one approval, exclude the author, and reset approvals after a push when changes should receive a fresh review.

### Agent Review

This gate evaluates unresolved runner findings on the latest push. The default `trail-review` runner produces findings with `high`, `medium`, or `low` severity. Choose the severity threshold that matches your team's merge policy.
Review each blocking finding and fix, resolve, or dismiss it. After a new push, findings tied to older code may become stale. Current findings remain open until they are resolved or dismissed.

### Checks

This gate evaluates CI checks reported through GitHub. Choose either:

* The checks GitHub marks as required.
* Specific check names you want to require.

Trails currently use a backing GitHub pull request for CI. Configure the checks your team needs before merging, such as its existing test and build checks.

## Review Gate Status on a Trail

Open the Trail's Gates section to see which requirements have passed and which are pending or blocking. Address the underlying requirement: update the branch, get an approval, handle findings, or investigate failing CI checks.

Select **Approve** when your review is complete. Once all blocking gates pass, select **Merge**.

If a blocking gate needs to be bypassed, only a person permitted by the repository's bypass configuration can do so. Every bypass is recorded on the Trail.

---
type: 'Concept'
title: 'Garantias verificables y limites de confianza'
description: 'Alcance real del tablero, referencia aprobada, evidencia de seguridad y migracion.'
tags: ['security', 'ccdd', 'reference']
---

# Garantias de verificacion

Complementa la [validacion](./validacion.md) y la [supervision humana](./supervision-humana.md). Un proceso exitoso, un test reconocido y una decision correcta de producto son propiedades distintas.

## Tablero local

Requiere Node 24 o posterior y Python. El lanzador imprime una URL autenticada con token en el fragmento; abrir esa URL, no solo el puerto. El navegador guarda el token en sessionStorage y elimina el fragmento. El servidor escucha exclusivamente en 127.0.0.1, exige Bearer en las APIs y rechaza origenes ajenos. Quien tenga el token puede ejecutar los comandos de los contratos locales; debe ser un operador de confianza. No es un sandbox ni un servicio multiusuario.

HTTP y MCP comparten el mismo ejecutor. Este valida el contrato con el parser Python canonico y toma de el test_command, target y tests; no ejecuta el comando arbitrario recibido al crear una tarea. Resuelve rutas reales dentro del proyecto y conserva cwd, comando y hashes SHA-256 del contrato, target y oraculo. Rechaza evidencia si esos archivos cambian durante la ejecucion o antes de cerrar/generar un reporte. Cambiar comando o contrato invalida la evidencia; nuevos requisitos humanos tambien la invalidan.

La evidencia cubre esos tres archivos. No cubre automaticamente dependencias transitivas, servicios externos, herramientas ni toda la revision del proyecto. La salida del runner reconoce totales de Node TAP/spec y unittest; una salida no reconocida conserva cero tests y no habilita done. Un proceso puede terminar correctamente sin ejecutar tests. El codigo hostil puede falsificar salida: estos controles presuponen un ejecutor y oraculo confiables.

## Vault

El piloto de [autoridad local](./data_models/local-authority.md) aplica permisos antes
de operaciones cerradas y limita ambitos delegados. Es independiente del runner del
tablero: no convierte sus comandos arbitrarios en operaciones aisladas.

El archivo .env.local del proyecto guarda valores en texto. Se inyectan solo al subproceso; no se exportan globalmente desde el flujo HTTP/MCP. Se redactan coincidencias exactas de valores conocidos en stdout/stderr antes de devolver o almacenar la salida. Esto no protege valores codificados, fragmentados o enviados por red. El codigo ejecutado y quien pueda leer el archivo pueden obtener los secretos. Para acceso ciego real se necesita un proxy de operaciones delimitadas con credenciales fuera del proceso controlado por el agente.

## Referencia aprobada

El hash tests_sha256 detecta diferencias respecto al contrato actual. El perfil
`standard` y el CI de pull requests comparan todos los contratos y sus oráculos
con una referencia aprobada, incluidas altas y bajas. Para revisar una tarea:

```sh
python scripts/validate_baseline.py knowledge/contracts/mi-tarea.md --approved-ref COMMIT_APROBADO
```

La referencia es obligatoria, sin default HEAD en `standard`/`strict`. Se
comparan contrato y archivo tests declarado en el contrato aprobado,
normalizando LF. La herramienta no modifica ni re-sella archivos. El commit
aprobado debe existir localmente; en CI se usa checkout con historial completo.
El CI nativo de pull requests y de `push` a `main` exige una entrada revisada
para el árbol Git exacto del candidato en `KDD_APPROVAL_REGISTRY`; el
[registro externo](approval-registry.md) define su formato y operación.
El workflow reutilizable acepta `approval_registry` o los inputs explícitos
`approved_baseline_ref` y `quality_approved_ref`, sin mezclar ambos modos.
El selector exporta las referencias seleccionadas como
`KDD_APPROVED_BASELINE_REF` y `KDD_QUALITY_APPROVED_REF`; las variables globales
antiguas no sustituyen una entrada ausente. Sin aprobación aplicable falla.
No usa el SHA de la rama base ni el commit que está validando como aprobación
automática. El workflow comprueba las referencias antes de ejecutar los
`test_command` y la suite del PR. Usa `contents: read` y el checkout no
persiste credenciales.

En este repositorio, la protección de `main` exige además `trusted-pr-gate`.
Su workflow `pull_request_target` usa código de `main` y lee el merge propuesto
como objetos Git, sin ejecutar archivos del PR. Compara contratos y oráculos
con la referencia aprobada y rechaza cambios a workflows o validadores
protegidos, incluso si el PR intenta aprobarse con su propio SHA. Al clonar
la plantilla, la configuración de protección de GitHub no se hereda: hay que
exigir este check explícitamente para obtener esa garantía. La herramienta
no autentica por sí sola la aprobación humana; quien administra la variable
y la protección de rama sigue siendo parte de la raíz de confianza.

## Inventario publicado en Pages

El [protocolo de inventario](./pages-ci-inventory.md) vincula el contador a
los reportes reales de dos pasadas por SO. El despliegue exige igualdad de
IDs entre Ubuntu/Windows y discovery local, con el mismo run, intento, SHA y
runtime revisado. Un import fallido, inventario incompleto o manifest
incompatible aborta antes de crear el bundle. Un preview de PR solo acredita
discovery y build; las suites posteriores conservan su veredicto independiente.

El conteo incluye IDs omitidos con motivo; no equivale a pruebas pasadas ni
a cobertura de codigo. El JSON no autentica la aprobacion humana: su
procedencia depende del workflow, evento y transporte de artifacts revisados.
El bundle HTML del PR no se reutiliza para desplegar. La
[guia operativa](../site/README.md) explica los modos y diagnosticos; el
[estado fechado](./estado-actual-kdd.md) distingue implementacion local y
publicacion comprobada.

## Cierre de contratos de proyecto

`validate_completion.py` impide que un reporte nuevo cierre un spec con
checkboxes pendientes o sin evidencia para todos sus criterios. El manifiesto
`CONTRACT-NN-EVIDENCE.json` registra el estado y enlaza un run de CI; el
reporte debe enlazar al mismo run. Es una comprobacion determinista de
coherencia entre artefactos. No consulta GitHub para autenticar el resultado
del run. El workflow ejecuta despues `verify_completion_runs.py`, que consulta
GitHub con permiso `actions: read` y confirma que ese run anterior termino en
exito para el SHA, repositorio y workflow declarados.

En un cierre nuevo, cada checkbox del spec lleva un ID como `[AC-1]` o
`[CI-1]` y se marca `[x]`. El manifiesto vecino al reporte usa este formato:

```json
{
  "schema_version": 1,
  "spec": "specs/CONTRACT-34-ejemplo.md",
  "state": "verified_in_ci",
  "ci": {
    "run_url": "https://github.com/OWNER/REPO/actions/runs/12345",
    "head_sha": "0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef01234567"
  },
  "criteria": {
    "AC-1": {"status": "locally_verified", "evidence": "registro de la prueba"},
    "CI-1": {"status": "verified_in_ci", "evidence": "https://github.com/OWNER/REPO/actions/runs/12345"}
  }
}
```

Haz que el reporte enlace al spec y al mismo URL del run. Agrega la tabla
`## Resultado por criterio` con columnas `ID | Estado | Evidencia`: cada fila
debe coincidir exactamente con el manifiesto JSON. Copia
`docs/reports/TEMPLATE-EVIDENCE.json` y `TEMPLATE-REPORT.md` como punto de
partida. Los workflows validan los cierres aun sin `completion-legacy.json`, usando el repositorio
del contexto de CI y cero excepciones. Para importar cierres historicos,
configura `repository` en esa politica como `OWNER/REPO` y protege el archivo
con revision de rama: quien pueda editarlo puede declarar un nuevo par como
legado y evitar el control de cierre.

El cierre usa **dos commits** para evitar que un workflow certifique su propio
resultado:

1. Publica el commit de implementacion con el spec abierto y sin reporte de
   cierre. Espera a que `validate-contracts` termine exitosamente.
2. En un commit posterior, marca los criterios cumplidos y agrega el reporte,
   manifiesto de evidencia y entrada de CHANGELOG. En `ci.head_sha` y
   `ci.run_url` apunta al run del commit anterior. No cambies codigo ni
   oraculos en este segundo commit.

# Gates

> Configure the requirements a Trail must satisfy before it can merge.

## What Are Gates?

Gates are merge requirements for a Trail. They bring branch freshness, human review, agent findings, and CI checks into one place so your team can see what is satisfied, pending, or blocking a merge.

While [Agents](https://docs.entire.com/guides/trails/agents.md) produce automated evaluations, Gates apply your repository's merge policy to the relevant evidence, including unresolved review findings and check results.

## Configure Gates

With repository admin permission:

1. Open your repository in entire.com.
2. Select **Settings** then **Gates**.
3. Turn on **Enable gates**.
4. Enable the Gates that you need for your repository.
5. Configure the requirements for each enabled gate.
6. Choose who may bypass a blocking gate.

Start with the requirements your team already uses for pull requests. Set up and merge the `trail-review` runner before making **Agent review** blocking.

[Configure Gates](https://customer-0x5hsk8lh27fm00g.cloudflarestream.com/fa86858d668db71f2eab5aed5b29fb35/iframe)

### Up to Date

This gate checks whether the Trail's branch is current with its base branch. You need to configure whether to allow a clean merge when the branch is behind. Use a blocking requirement when your team needs changes evaluated against the latest base before merging.

### Human Review

This gate evaluates approvals submitted on the Trail. Configure:

* The minimum number of approvals.
* Whether the Trail author's approval counts.
* Whether new pushes reset existing approvals.

For example, require one approval, exclude the author, and reset approvals after a push when changes should receive a fresh review.

### Agent Review

This gate evaluates unresolved runner findings on the latest push. The default `trail-review` runner produces findings with `high`, `medium`, or `low` severity. Choose the severity threshold that matches your team's merge policy.
Review each blocking finding and fix, resolve, or dismiss it. After a new push, findings tied to older code may become stale. Current findings remain open until they are resolved or dismissed.

### Checks

This gate evaluates CI checks reported through GitHub. Choose either:

* The checks GitHub marks as required.
* Specific check names you want to require.

Trails currently use a backing GitHub pull request for CI. Configure the checks your team needs before merging, such as its existing test and build checks.

## Review Gate Status on a Trail

Open the Trail's Gates section to see which requirements have passed and which are pending or blocking. Address the underlying requirement: update the branch, get an approval, handle findings, or investigate failing CI checks.

Select **Approve** when your review is complete. Once all blocking gates pass, select **Merge**.

If a blocking gate needs to be bypassed, only a person permitted by the repository's bypass configuration can do so. Every bypass is recorded on the Trail.

# Agents

> Configure automated Trail evaluations and write custom agents for your repository.

## What Are Agents?

Agents are configurable AI jobs that review changes in a Trail and evaluate them using customizable instructions. They run in isolated cloud sandboxes and can produce summaries, identify code review findings, or report evaluation scores.
Agents can evaluate different aspects of a change, such as Confidence, Risk, Security, and Drift. Each Agent can report a score and flag issues that need attention as Findings.
[Gates](https://docs.entire.com/guides/trails/gates.md) define the requirements that determine whether a Trail can merge. Once configured, your Agents will look something like this:

![Trail change showing code review, security review, Slop, and monitor results](https://mintcdn.com/entire/7Crxbl28PbL5RtNq/images/trails-agent-evaluations.png?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=7Crxbl28PbL5RtNq\&q=85\&s=4610de86a7092c06ee944efba8aa4ad5)

Agent evaluation results on a Trail change.

## How Agents Work

With Agents and Auto build on push enabled in repository settings, pushing changes to a Trail branch triggers the configured Agents. Each Agent uses its instructions and selected configuration to evaluate the changes.
Entire displays the results on the Trail. Reviewers can use the scores to focus their review, investigate Findings, and push fixes for another evaluation.
The available preset Agents include:

* **Code review:** Reviews every push and flags what needs to be fixed.
* **Security review:** Checks every change for anything that could lead to a security breach in your codebase.
* **Slop:** Catches sloppy patterns and drift before you merge them on your main codebase.

![Entire agent presets for code review, security review, and detecting sloppy patterns and drift](https://mintcdn.com/entire/7Crxbl28PbL5RtNq/images/trails-agent-presets.png?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=7Crxbl28PbL5RtNq\&q=85\&s=93c0acfa9a7304c2ba1d23c2e9814313)

Preset agents available on the project's Agents page.

The default monitor scores range from 0 to 100. You can read their rationale alongside the score and the underlying code. Here’s an example of how it looks:

![Security score dialog showing a score of 5 percent, supporting rationale, and evaluation history](https://mintcdn.com/entire/7Crxbl28PbL5RtNq/images/trails-security-score-rationale.png?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=7Crxbl28PbL5RtNq\&q=85\&s=7d4f9ca58baad806be05037e7b371482)

A Security monitor score with its rationale and history.

## Set Up Your First Agent

To create your first Agent:

1. Navigate to your project on Entire.com.
2. Open your project and go to **Agents** then click on **Manage Agents**.

[Open project Agents](https://customer-0x5hsk8lh27fm00g.cloudflarestream.com/e24c2efca1b9ae12221bcd13cf14b677/iframe)

3. Choose an Agent from the list of presets and click **Enable** to start using it.

[Enable a preset agent](https://customer-0x5hsk8lh27fm00g.cloudflarestream.com/87c891fe2bf2042b7c4e1b12c7e19248/iframe)

## Creating a Custom Agent

If you want to create an Agent with your own configuration, follow these steps:

Click **New agent**. Under Agent, give it a name and description. Select the harness, model, reasoning effort, and timeout. Then write the Instructions describing what the Agent should review and evaluate.
For example, you can create a Migration Risk Agent to evaluate database migration changes.
Under **Agent**, enter the following details:

* Name: Migration Risk
* Description: Evaluates database migration changes for potential deployment and rollback risks.
* Harness, model, reasoning effort, and timeout: Select the configuration that meets your evaluation requirements.

Instructions:

```text theme={null}
Evaluate database migration risk in the Trail's changes. Inspect changed migrations and related application code for destructive operations, locking, compatibility during rollout, and rollback safety.
Score risk from 0 to 100, where higher values indicate greater potential damage. If no migration-related changes exist, return 0 and explain why.
Provide a short rationale explaining the evidence behind the score.
```

Configure the signal the Agent reports by selecting its value type and polarity. The value type determines how the score is represented, while the polarity determines whether higher or lower values are better.

Under **Trigger**, choose when the Agent runs. You can select Trail branch pushed, Run manually, or Recurring schedule.

Under **Repositories**, select at least one repository where the Agent should run.

[Create a custom agent](https://customer-0x5hsk8lh27fm00g.cloudflarestream.com/54a12ce490642658eceaddaa1a963784/iframe)

Leave the **Active** toggle enabled and click **Create agent**.
After it is successfully created, you should see it under the Agents tab as in the image below.

![Agents page listing an active Payments reviewer with its repositories and selected model](https://mintcdn.com/entire/7Crxbl28PbL5RtNq/images/trails-custom-agent.png?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=7Crxbl28PbL5RtNq\&q=85\&s=b5305477d17ae14bdf06b753c67850bc)

A custom agent listed on the project’s Agents page.

Once configured, the Agent can evaluate changes, report a score, and flag issues as Findings.

## Understand the Agent Configuration

| Setting | Purpose |
| - | - |
| Name and description | Identify the Agent and describe what it evaluates. |
| Harness | Select the coding agent environment used for evaluation. |
| Model | Choose the AI model used by the Agent. |
| Reasoning effort | Configure how much reasoning the model uses during evaluation. |
| Timeout | Set the maximum time allowed for an evaluation. |
| Instructions | Define what the Agent should review and how it should evaluate changes. |
| Value type | Define how the Agent's evaluation score is represented. |

## Agent Insights

Agent Insights helps you understand how coding agents use tokens across your Trails and repositories. You can track token consumption by activity, compare usage across models, and identify changes that required more agent effort than expected.

### How to Enable Agent Insights

To start tracking agent token usage, go to the Plugins tab in your project and find the Agent Insights extension.
Click Install, select the repositories on Entire where you want to enable Agent Insights, and click Install again.

[Install Agent Insights](https://customer-0x5hsk8lh27fm00g.cloudflarestream.com/0445a8cbe2442fc3528bde0ce38fcc3e/iframe)

### View Token Usage in a Trail

Once it is enabled, open a Trail and navigate to Sessions to see a breakdown of token usage across agent activities, such as understanding code, building, checking, reworking, reviewing, and coordinating.
Hover over the visualization to see the percentage of tokens spent on each activity. This helps you understand how the agent worked on a change and whether it spent more tokens implementing changes or making repeated fixes.

![Sessions token usage bar with a tooltip showing percentages for understanding, building, checking, reworking, shipping, coordinating, and reviewing](https://mintcdn.com/entire/7Crxbl28PbL5RtNq/images/trails-agent-insights-activities.png?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=7Crxbl28PbL5RtNq\&q=85\&s=6554d6bb00f76b360bd9249e07058710)

Token usage by activity within a Trail’s Sessions section.

### View Agent Insights in Repository Analytics

Open your repository's existing Analytics page and scroll to the Agent Insights section.
The Analytics page is available independently of the plugin. Enabling Agent Insights adds more detailed token usage metrics across merged Trails through three visualizations:

* **Token Volume by Model:** Track daily token consumption grouped by the models used.
* **Tokens vs. Lines Changed:** Compare token usage against the number of lines modified in each Trail. This helps identify which Trails consume the most tokens.
* **Tokens by Activity:** Compare token usage across activities between the current and previous week to understand how agent behavior changes over time.

You can use these metrics to identify unusual token consumption, understand which activities require the most effort, and compare agent usage across Trails.

# Garantias de verificacion

Complementa la [validacion](./validacion.md) y la [supervision humana](./supervision-humana.md). Un proceso exitoso, un test reconocido y una decision correcta de producto son propiedades distintas.

## Tablero local

Requiere Node 24 o posterior y Python. El lanzador imprime una URL autenticada con token en el fragmento; abrir esa URL, no solo el puerto. El navegador guarda el token en sessionStorage y elimina el fragmento. El servidor escucha exclusivamente en 127.0.0.1, exige Bearer en las APIs y rechaza origenes ajenos. Quien tenga el token puede ejecutar los comandos de los contratos locales; debe ser un operador de confianza. No es un sandbox ni un servicio multiusuario.

HTTP y MCP comparten el mismo ejecutor. Este valida el contrato con el parser Python canonico y toma de el test_command, target y tests; no ejecuta el comando arbitrario recibido al crear una tarea. Resuelve rutas reales dentro del proyecto y conserva cwd, comando y hashes SHA-256 del contrato, target y oraculo. Rechaza evidencia si esos archivos cambian durante la ejecucion o antes de cerrar/generar un reporte. Cambiar comando o contrato invalida la evidencia; nuevos requisitos humanos tambien la invalidan.

La evidencia cubre esos tres archivos. No cubre automaticamente dependencias transitivas, servicios externos, herramientas ni toda la revision del proyecto. La salida del runner reconoce totales de Node TAP/spec y unittest; una salida no reconocida conserva cero tests y no habilita done. Un proceso puede terminar correctamente sin ejecutar tests. El codigo hostil puede falsificar salida: estos controles presuponen un ejecutor y oraculo confiables.

## Vault

El piloto de [autoridad local](./data_models/local-authority.md) aplica permisos antes
de operaciones cerradas y limita ambitos delegados. Es independiente del runner del
tablero: no convierte sus comandos arbitrarios en operaciones aisladas.

El archivo .env.local del proyecto guarda valores en texto. Se inyectan solo al subproceso; no se exportan globalmente desde el flujo HTTP/MCP. Se redactan coincidencias exactas de valores conocidos en stdout/stderr antes de devolver o almacenar la salida. Esto no protege valores codificados, fragmentados o enviados por red. El codigo ejecutado y quien pueda leer el archivo pueden obtener los secretos. Para acceso ciego real se necesita un proxy de operaciones delimitadas con credenciales fuera del proceso controlado por el agente.

## Referencia aprobada

El hash tests_sha256 detecta diferencias respecto al contrato actual. El perfil
`standard` y el CI de pull requests comparan todos los contratos y sus oráculos
con una referencia aprobada, incluidas altas y bajas. Para revisar una tarea:

```sh
python scripts/validate_baseline.py knowledge/contracts/mi-tarea.md --approved-ref COMMIT_APROBADO
```

La referencia es obligatoria, sin default HEAD en `standard`/`strict`. Se
comparan contrato y archivo tests declarado en el contrato aprobado,
normalizando LF. La herramienta no modifica ni re-sella archivos. El commit
aprobado debe existir localmente; en CI se usa checkout con historial completo.
El CI nativo de pull requests y de `push` a `main` exige una entrada revisada
para el árbol Git exacto del candidato en `KDD_APPROVAL_REGISTRY`; el
[registro externo](approval-registry.md) define su formato y operación.
El workflow reutilizable acepta `approval_registry` o los inputs explícitos
`approved_baseline_ref` y `quality_approved_ref`, sin mezclar ambos modos.
El selector exporta las referencias seleccionadas como
`KDD_APPROVED_BASELINE_REF` y `KDD_QUALITY_APPROVED_REF`; las variables globales
antiguas no sustituyen una entrada ausente. Sin aprobación aplicable falla.
No usa el SHA de la rama base ni el commit que está validando como aprobación
automática. El workflow comprueba las referencias antes de ejecutar los
`test_command` y la suite del PR. Usa `contents: read` y el checkout no
persiste credenciales.

En este repositorio, la protección de `main` exige además `trusted-pr-gate`.
Su workflow `pull_request_target` usa código de `main` y lee el merge propuesto
como objetos Git, sin ejecutar archivos del PR. Compara contratos y oráculos
con la referencia aprobada y rechaza cambios a workflows o validadores
protegidos, incluso si el PR intenta aprobarse con su propio SHA. Al clonar
la plantilla, la configuración de protección de GitHub no se hereda: hay que
exigir este check explícitamente para obtener esa garantía. La herramienta
no autentica por sí sola la aprobación humana; quien administra la variable
y la protección de rama sigue siendo parte de la raíz de confianza.

## Inventario publicado en Pages

El [protocolo de inventario](./pages-ci-inventory.md) vincula el contador a
los reportes reales de dos pasadas por SO. El despliegue exige igualdad de
IDs entre Ubuntu/Windows y discovery local, con el mismo run, intento, SHA y
runtime revisado. Un import fallido, inventario incompleto o manifest
incompatible aborta antes de crear el bundle. Un preview de PR solo acredita
discovery y build; las suites posteriores conservan su veredicto independiente.

El conteo incluye IDs omitidos con motivo; no equivale a pruebas pasadas ni
a cobertura de codigo. El JSON no autentica la aprobacion humana: su
procedencia depende del workflow, evento y transporte de artifacts revisados.
El bundle HTML del PR no se reutiliza para desplegar. La
[guia operativa](../site/README.md) explica los modos y diagnosticos; el
[estado fechado](./estado-actual-kdd.md) distingue implementacion local y
publicacion comprobada.

## Cierre de contratos de proyecto

`validate_completion.py` impide que un reporte nuevo cierre un spec con
checkboxes pendientes o sin evidencia para todos sus criterios. El manifiesto
`CONTRACT-NN-EVIDENCE.json` registra el estado y enlaza un run de CI; el
reporte debe enlazar al mismo run. Es una comprobacion determinista de
coherencia entre artefactos. No consulta GitHub para autenticar el resultado
del run. El workflow ejecuta despues `verify_completion_runs.py`, que consulta
GitHub con permiso `actions: read` y confirma que ese run anterior termino en
exito para el SHA, repositorio y workflow declarados.

En un cierre nuevo, cada checkbox del spec lleva un ID como `[AC-1]` o
`[CI-1]` y se marca `[x]`. El manifiesto vecino al reporte usa este formato:

```json
{
  "schema_version": 1,
  "spec": "specs/CONTRACT-34-ejemplo.md",
  "state": "verified_in_ci",
  "ci": {
    "run_url": "https://github.com/OWNER/REPO/actions/runs/12345",
    "head_sha": "0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef01234567"
  },
  "criteria": {
    "AC-1": {"status": "locally_verified", "evidence": "registro de la prueba"},
    "CI-1": {"status": "verified_in_ci", "evidence": "https://github.com/OWNER/REPO/actions/runs/12345"}
  }
}
```

Haz que el reporte enlace al spec y al mismo URL del run. Agrega la tabla
`## Resultado por criterio` con columnas `ID | Estado | Evidencia`: cada fila
debe coincidir exactamente con el manifiesto JSON. Copia
`docs/reports/TEMPLATE-EVIDENCE.json` y `TEMPLATE-REPORT.md` como punto de
partida. Los workflows validan los cierres aun sin `completion-legacy.json`, usando el repositorio
del contexto de CI y cero excepciones. Para importar cierres historicos,
configura `repository` en esa politica como `OWNER/REPO` y protege el archivo
con revision de rama: quien pueda editarlo puede declarar un nuevo par como
legado y evitar el control de cierre.

El cierre usa **dos commits** para evitar que un workflow certifique su propio
resultado:

1. Publica el commit de implementacion con el spec abierto y sin reporte de
   cierre. Espera a que `validate-contracts` termine exitosamente.
2. En un commit posterior, marca los criterios cumplidos y agrega el reporte,
   manifiesto de evidencia y entrada de CHANGELOG. En `ci.head_sha` y
   `ci.run_url` apunta al run del commit anterior. No cambies codigo ni
   oraculos en este segundo commit.
"}}

También encontré una diferencia entre el mensaje comercial de privacidad y la documentación: la redacción de secretos es de mejor esfuerzo y las sesiones pueden publicarse con el repositorio. Para KDD, la oportunidad más clara parece ser complementar la trazabilidad y la memoria con sus controles deterministas.

Para KDD, la oportunidad más clara parece ser complementar la trazabilidad y la memoria con sus controles deterministas.

**Entire convierte el contexto del desarrollo con IA en parte del repositorio:** conserva las sesiones, las vincula con cambios de código y permite reutilizarlas para buscar, revisar y continuar trabajo. Su propuesta tiene valor especialmente para equipos que usan varios agentes y generan más cambios de los que pueden revisar cómodamente.

Revisé el sitio, la documentación y sus repositorios públicos. El análisis es documental; no instalé el producto ni reproduje sus benchmarks.

**El producto tiene cuatro piezas principales:**

| Pieza | Qué aporta |
|---|---|
| **Checkpoints** | Vinculan commits con prompts, respuestas y herramientas utilizadas durante la sesión. |
| **Continuous Memory** | Combina sesiones, documentación, decisiones y un grafo del código para recuperar contexto. |
| **Trails** | Agrupan intención, cambios entre repositorios, revisiones, resultados de CI y aprobaciones. |
| **Git distribuido** | Ofrece alojamiento propio y mirrors regionales de repositorios de GitHub. |

Estas capacidades están descritas en su [documentación general](https://docs.entire.com/).

**Lo más convincente es la continuidad entre agentes.** Recuperar por qué se tomó una decisión puede evitar investigaciones repetidas y facilitar relevos entre personas y modelos. Además, la captura local funciona en repositorios Git sin necesitar una cuenta; el CLI es MIT y permite adoptar esa parte antes de incorporar el alojamiento. Eso reduce la fricción inicial. [Repositorio del CLI](https://github.com/entireio/cli)

Veo tres puntos que requieren una lectura cuidadosa:

- **Los indicadores de riesgo necesitan interpretación.** Sus monitores producen puntuaciones mediante agentes configurables, con instrucciones y modelos seleccionados. Un “7 % de riesgo” debe entenderse como una señal de evaluación; la documentación revisada no establece que sea una probabilidad estadísticamente calibrada. [Evaluaciones de agentes](https://docs.entire.com/guides/trails/agents.md)
- **Los números de rendimiento tienen un alcance concreto.** El “hasta 89×” corresponde a throughput de operaciones Git; el ahorro de “hasta 71 %” depende del escenario de recuperación de contexto. No permiten deducir una mejora equivalente en todo el desarrollo. ForgeMark documenta además cómo influyen concurrencia, latencia y límites del proveedor. [ForgeMark](https://github.com/entireio/forgemark), [Entire Graph](https://github.com/entireio/entire-graph)
- **El mensaje comercial de privacidad es demasiado absoluto.** La portada afirma que los datos sensibles permanecen en la máquina, mientras la documentación explica que la redacción es de mejor esfuerzo, que los checkpoints pueden subirse al remoto y que las imágenes no se escanean. En un repositorio público, las sesiones publicadas también son accesibles. [Seguridad y privacidad](https://docs.entire.com/security)

**Como sitio comercial, comunica amplitud y ambición.** La estética oscura, la jerarquía tipográfica y las demostraciones del producto encajan con su público técnico. Sin embargo, presenta muchos conceptos desde el inicio: forge, Trails, memoria, búsqueda, CLI y CI. Mi recomendación editorial sería explicar antes un recorrido concreto —hacer un cambio, capturarlo, revisarlo y retomarlo— y mostrar con mayor claridad qué requiere cuenta, alojamiento o servicios adicionales. Tampoco encontré tarifas y límites suficientes en las páginas revisadas para calcular el coste de adopción.

**Para tu proyecto KDD, hay solapamiento y una integración posible.** Entire ya dispone de gates para checks de CI, aprobaciones humanas y hallazgos de agentes. La diferencia relevante está en qué evidencia exige cada control. [Gates de Entire](https://docs.entire.com/guides/trails/gates.md)

KDD aporta contratos, oráculos congelados y comparación con referencias aprobadas, con límites de confianza documentados en sus [garantías de verificación](D:/Repo/kdd_2/knowledge/verification-guarantees.md). Entire aporta captura automática de sesiones, búsqueda histórica y una interfaz integrada de revisión.

# Reglas para Agentes de IA

Si eres un agente de IA interactuando con este repositorio, debes acatar las siguientes reglas:

1. **Metodología KDD Obligatoria**: Este repositorio utiliza Knowledge-Driven Development. Antes de escribir código, debes leer los contratos en `knowledge/contracts/` y la spec normativa de los nodos OKF en `knowledge/OKF-SPEC.md`.
2. **Carga la Skill Local**: Tienes disponible la skill `kdd-okf-ccdd-hybrid` en el directorio `.agents/skills/`. Debes adoptarla en tu contexto para entender cómo generar y validar los contratos híbridos OKF-CCDD.
3. **No dupliques contexto**: Utiliza enlaces de markdown relativos a `knowledge/` cuando necesites explicar el porqué de una implementación.
4. **Validación Determinista (dos niveles)**: la referencia canónica completa (niveles, gate multi-lenguaje, export, `tc-tests-frozen`) está en [knowledge/validacion.md](../knowledge/validacion.md) — léela antes de validar; esta regla no la duplica. Resumen: nivel 1 (obligatorio) = `python scripts/validate_contracts.py knowledge/contracts` (incluye el sello obligatorio `tests_sha256` del oráculo; sellar con `--hash`) + `python scripts/validate_specs.py specs` + `python scripts/validate_okf.py knowledge` (estructura/frontmatter de nodos OKF) + `python scripts/lint_ascii.py scripts` + `python scripts/validate_rules.py <dir>` (rule contracts, capa opcional) + `python scripts/validate_skills.py skills .agents/skills` (skills de agente, capa opcional) + `python scripts/validate_changelog.py` (coherencia CHANGELOG↔reportes, capa opcional) + `python scripts/validate_ux_page.py examples/ux-page` (UX/accesibilidad mecánica sobre paginas HTML autocontenidas, capa opcional) + `python scripts/validate_diagrams.py <dir>` (diagramas Mermaid flowchart verificados contra un .diagram-contract.json declarativo, capa opcional) + `python scripts/validate_test_commands.py <contracts_dir> <repo_root>` (corre el test_command real de cada contrato y falla si algun exit code no es 0, Nivel 1 obligatorio) + `python scripts/scan_secrets.py <dir>` (escaneo determinista de credenciales filtradas por prefijo de proveedor conocido, capa opcional) + el `test_command` del contrato, local y en CI (matriz dual-OS, suite 2x); nivel 2 (opcional) = gate CCDD vía MCP `ccdd-complexity` (`lint_task_contract`, `run_integration_gate`) sobre el export de `scripts/export_gate_contract.py`. Ningún contrato se considera terminado hasta que pase el nivel 1.
5. **Precedencia del Budget**: ver [knowledge/validacion.md](../knowledge/validacion.md) — con gate manda su config firmada (el `budget` del frontmatter solo puede ser <=); sin gate, el `budget` es declarativo y el validador solo verifica su presencia.
6. **Ciclo de Vida del Contrato**: `draft` -> `validated` -> `implemented` -> `verified`; detalle y evidencia requerida en [knowledge/validacion.md](../knowledge/validacion.md).
7. **Contexto presupuestado (CCDD Nivel 2)**: Antes de implementar una tarea delegada, ensambla su contexto con `python scripts/assemble_context.py ccdd/context.json "<tarea>"` (añade `-v` para el contexto completo). El reporte de slots/guardrails que imprime forma parte de la evidencia y se pega en `.agents/logs/<task>-REPORT.md`. Un guardrail `on_fail: abort` (exit 2) bloquea la tarea: no continúes hasta resolverlo. La doc del ensamblador vive en el script; aquí solo se referencia por ruta.

Este archivo es la fuente única de verdad para cualquier agente, sea cual sea la herramienta que lo hospeda. `.cursorrules`, `.github/copilot-instructions.md`, `.clinerules` y `.windsurfrules` en la raíz del repo son punteros delgados a este mismo archivo (convención de cada herramienta), no una copia — si hay divergencia, este archivo manda. Para un humano que revisa lo que produjo un agente, ver [knowledge/supervision-humana.md](../knowledge/supervision-humana.md).

## Herramientas de diagnóstico opt-in (NO son gates)

Nivel 2 tambien dispone de [integracion nativa](../knowledge/native-level2.md)
para funciones Python. Las menciones de MCP en el resumen anterior describen una
via disponible, no un requisito. Si el proyecto exige Nivel 2, su ausencia/error
bloquea: no sustituirlo silenciosamente por Nivel 1. El perfil nativo identifica
su politica por commit; no autentica firmas de umbrales.

Tres herramientas de diagnóstico local, opt-in, que **no son gates y no corren en CI**: Nivel 1 sigue siendo **19 gates** y el conteo no cambia. Documentación a fondo en [knowledge/validacion.md](../knowledge/validacion.md) (secciones "Preflight", "Auditor de seals débiles" y "Recetas de arreglo por rule-id").

- `python scripts/preflight.py [--repo-root DIR] [--contract NAME]` — dry-run de los 20 gates (19 de Nivel 1 + `validate_attestation` local-only); una línea `PASS`/`FAIL`/`TIMEOUT` por gate + resumen `N/20`. Úsalo **antes de delegar o empezar trabajo**, para no entregarle a un agente un repo que ya rompe un gate. Modo `--contract`: 3 chequeos de un task contract (frontmatter, sello, `test_command`).
- `python scripts/audit_seals.py [contracts_dir] [--repo-root DIR] [--strict]` — auditor ADVISORY de "seals débiles": detecta oráculos congelados que el sello (`tests_sha256`) certifica como íntegros pero que no pueden fallar (6 reglas `WEAK_*`). Úsalo **al autorar o revisar un oráculo, antes de sellarlo**. Sin `--strict` siempre exit 0 (advisory); con `--strict`, exit 1 si hay findings.
- `python scripts/rule_hints.py <RULE_ID> | --all | --json` — la **receta de arreglo** de cualquiera de los 107 rule-ids que emiten los validadores. Los gates dicen *qué* falló (`clave requerida ausente: type`), no *qué hacer*: esto es lo segundo. Úsalo **cuando un gate te falla y el mensaje no te dice cómo arreglarlo**, en vez de tantear. Atajo: `python scripts/preflight.py --agent` corre el preflight y cada gate en rojo ya arrastra la receta de sus rule-ids, así que normalmente ese es el único comando que necesitas.
## Aprobacion integrada de nuevos proyectos

Al instanciar un proyecto nuevo, seguir [quality-approval](../knowledge/quality-approval.md): definir politica y oraculos antes de implementar y usar verify_quality.py con referencia aprobada explicita como punto de aprobacion. Incluir checks funcionales, adversariales y de interfaz cuando corresponda. Nunca convertir un fallo inconcluso en deteccion de una mutacion ni elegir HEAD automaticamente para aprobar el trabajo actual.

# Reglas para Agentes de IA

Si eres un agente de IA interactuando con este repositorio, debes acatar las siguientes reglas:

1. **Metodología KDD Obligatoria**: Este repositorio utiliza Knowledge-Driven Development. Antes de escribir código, debes leer los contratos en `knowledge/contracts/` y la spec normativa de los nodos OKF en `knowledge/OKF-SPEC.md`.
2. **Carga la Skill Local**: Tienes disponible la skill `kdd-okf-ccdd-hybrid` en el directorio `.agents/skills/`. Debes adoptarla en tu contexto para entender cómo generar y validar los contratos híbridos OKF-CCDD.
3. **No dupliques contexto**: Utiliza enlaces de markdown relativos a `knowledge/` cuando necesites explicar el porqué de una implementación.
4. **Validación Determinista (dos niveles)**: la referencia canónica completa (niveles, gate multi-lenguaje, export, `tc-tests-frozen`) está en [knowledge/validacion.md](../knowledge/validacion.md) — léela antes de validar; esta regla no la duplica. Resumen: nivel 1 (obligatorio) = `python scripts/validate_contracts.py knowledge/contracts` (incluye el sello obligatorio `tests_sha256` del oráculo; sellar con `--hash`) + `python scripts/validate_specs.py specs` + `python scripts/validate_okf.py knowledge` (estructura/frontmatter de nodos OKF) + `python scripts/lint_ascii.py scripts` + `python scripts/validate_rules.py <dir>` (rule contracts, capa opcional) + `python scripts/validate_skills.py skills .agents/skills` (skills de agente, capa opcional) + `python scripts/validate_changelog.py` (coherencia CHANGELOG↔reportes, capa opcional) + `python scripts/validate_ux_page.py examples/ux-page` (UX/accesibilidad mecánica sobre paginas HTML autocontenidas, capa opcional) + `python scripts/validate_diagrams.py <dir>` (diagramas Mermaid flowchart verificados contra un .diagram-contract.json declarativo, capa opcional) + `python scripts/validate_test_commands.py <contracts_dir> <repo_root>` (corre el test_command real de cada contrato y falla si algun exit code no es 0, Nivel 1 obligatorio) + `python scripts/scan_secrets.py <dir>` (escaneo determinista de credenciales filtradas por prefijo de proveedor conocido, capa opcional) + el `test_command` del contrato, local y en CI (matriz dual-OS, suite 2x); nivel 2 (opcional) = gate CCDD vía MCP `ccdd-complexity` (`lint_task_contract`, `run_integration_gate`) sobre el export de `scripts/export_gate_contract.py`. Ningún contrato se considera terminado hasta que pase el nivel 1.
5. **Precedencia del Budget**: ver [knowledge/validacion.md](../knowledge/validacion.md) — con gate manda su config firmada (el `budget` del frontmatter solo puede ser <=); sin gate, el `budget` es declarativo y el validador solo verifica su presencia.
6. **Ciclo de Vida del Contrato**: `draft` -> `validated` -> `implemented` -> `verified`; detalle y evidencia requerida en [knowledge/validacion.md](../knowledge/validacion.md).
7. **Contexto presupuestado (CCDD Nivel 2)**: Antes de implementar una tarea delegada, ensambla su contexto con `python scripts/assemble_context.py ccdd/context.json "<tarea>"` (añade `-v` para el contexto completo). El reporte de slots/guardrails que imprime forma parte de la evidencia y se pega en `.agents/logs/<task>-REPORT.md`. Un guardrail `on_fail: abort` (exit 2) bloquea la tarea: no continúes hasta resolverlo. La doc del ensamblador vive en el script; aquí solo se referencia por ruta.

Este archivo es la fuente única de verdad para cualquier agente, sea cual sea la herramienta que lo hospeda. `.cursorrules`, `.github/copilot-instructions.md`, `.clinerules` y `.windsurfrules` en la raíz del repo son punteros delgados a este mismo archivo (convención de cada herramienta), no una copia — si hay divergencia, este archivo manda. Para un humano que revisa lo que produjo un agente, ver [knowledge/supervision-humana.md](../knowledge/supervision-humana.md).

## Herramientas de diagnóstico opt-in (NO son gates)

Nivel 2 tambien dispone de [integracion nativa](../knowledge/native-level2.md)
para funciones Python. Las menciones de MCP en el resumen anterior describen una
via disponible, no un requisito. Si el proyecto exige Nivel 2, su ausencia/error
bloquea: no sustituirlo silenciosamente por Nivel 1. El perfil nativo identifica
su politica por commit; no autentica firmas de umbrales.

Tres herramientas de diagnóstico local, opt-in, que **no son gates y no corren en CI**: Nivel 1 sigue siendo **19 gates** y el conteo no cambia. Documentación a fondo en [knowledge/validacion.md](../knowledge/validacion.md) (secciones "Preflight", "Auditor de seals débiles" y "Recetas de arreglo por rule-id").

- `python scripts/preflight.py [--repo-root DIR] [--contract NAME]` — dry-run de los 20 gates (19 de Nivel 1 + `validate_attestation` local-only); una línea `PASS`/`FAIL`/`TIMEOUT` por gate + resumen `N/20`. Úsalo **antes de delegar o empezar trabajo**, para no entregarle a un agente un repo que ya rompe un gate. Modo `--contract`: 3 chequeos de un task contract (frontmatter, sello, `test_command`).
- `python scripts/audit_seals.py [contracts_dir] [--repo-root DIR] [--strict]` — auditor ADVISORY de "seals débiles": detecta oráculos congelados que el sello (`tests_sha256`) certifica como íntegros pero que no pueden fallar (6 reglas `WEAK_*`). Úsalo **al autorar o revisar un oráculo, antes de sellarlo**. Sin `--strict` siempre exit 0 (advisory); con `--strict`, exit 1 si hay findings.
- `python scripts/rule_hints.py <RULE_ID> | --all | --json` — la **receta de arreglo** de cualquiera de los 107 rule-ids que emiten los validadores. Los gates dicen *qué* falló (`clave requerida ausente: type`), no *qué hacer*: esto es lo segundo. Úsalo **cuando un gate te falla y el mensaje no te dice cómo arreglarlo**, en vez de tantear. Atajo: `python scripts/preflight.py --agent` corre el preflight y cada gate en rojo ya arrastra la receta de sus rule-ids, así que normalmente ese es el único comando que necesitas.
## Aprobacion integrada de nuevos proyectos

Al instanciar un proyecto nuevo, seguir [quality-approval](../knowledge/quality-approval.md): definir politica y oraculos antes de implementar y usar verify_quality.py con referencia aprobada explicita como punto de aprobacion. Incluir checks funcionales, adversariales y de interfaz cuando corresponda. Nunca convertir un fallo inconcluso en deteccion de una mutacion ni elegir HEAD automaticamente para aprobar el trabajo actual.

# Codex

> Capture Codex transcripts, file changes, tokens, and subagent sessions with Entire

The Codex integration uses Codex's project-level hook system.

Follow [Set Up an Agent](https://docs.entire.com/agents/setup.md) for shared installation, verification, and troubleshooting steps.

## Add Codex

```bash theme={null}
entire agent add codex
codex
```

Entire writes `.codex/hooks.json`. Codex enables hooks by default beginning with version 0.124.0, so Entire does not create `.codex/config.toml` or set `codex_hooks = true`.

The hooks capture session boundaries, prompts, completed turns, file-changing tool calls, and subagent events. Entire reads the full conversation and token usage from Codex rollout files under `~/.codex/` or `CODEX_HOME`.

## Limitations

Ephemeral Codex runs may not provide a transcript path. Entire can process their hook events, but it cannot attach a full transcript without the rollout file.

Entire records the subagents that changed files, materializes their transcripts into the parent's next checkpoint, and attributes their files to the parent session. It skips a subagent that wrote nothing, and it does not yet roll subagent tokens up into the parent session's totals.

## Resume and Import

`entire session resume BRANCH` restores the recorded session data when needed and prints:

```bash theme={null}
codex resume SESSION_ID
```

Entire can import existing Codex transcripts from the previous 30 days as read-only checkpoints.

See the [`session resume` command reference](https://docs.entire.com/cli-reference/session#session-resume) for flags and additional behavior.

# OpenAI Docs

Provide current, cited OpenAI product, API, model, and Codex guidance. Read zero or one primary reference.

**First substantive action:** Search the user's exact requested official OpenAI documentation topic and any explicitly named model using a concise, topic-specific query of 2-6 essential terms. When an already-available direct official documentation search and page-retrieval capability is present, use it first: search, then fetch or open the matching official page before general web search. Otherwise, immediately use official-domain web search, then actually open or fetch the relevant official page. Complete this source order before reading a reference, inspecting local or repository files, running a Codex manual or model resolver, drafting a plan, or answering from memory. Use the actual fetched page, not a search snippet or an unopened link. If one official search or page does not establish the answer, search another appropriate official domain and actually open or fetch the result. Preserve the exact requested model; never substitute a newer model.

**Only exception:** An explicitly requested, genuinely broad, cross-topic Codex setup, orientation, or system-map synthesis may use the manual first when shell execution and an allowed temporary cache are available. Mixed Chat/Work/Codex comparisons are official documentation questions, not manual-first Codex requests.

For generic software tasks, answer the software task directly. OpenAI implementation, debugging, SDK, API, prompting, agent, and eval requests are not generic.

For a straightforward factual or citation-only request, follow the source order and do not read a route reference. ## Choose one primary route

Use the first matching route, and read its reference only when the requested task needs that specialized workflow:

- **Explicitly requested local documentation integration:** Read [integration guidance](references/mcp-diagnostics.md) only when the user explicitly requests that local integration.
- **Model migration, upgrades, or model-specific prompting:** Read [model-migration.md](references/model-migration.md) for actual migration planning, implementation, dynamic target resolution, or prompt changes. Preserve an explicitly requested target.
- **Model selection and comparisons:** Read [model-selection.md](references/model-selection.md) only when nuanced current, latest, default, cost, latency, quality, or modality tradeoffs need more guidance. Do not run a migration resolver for selection alone.
- **Product, API, ChatGPT Work, and mixed Chat/Work/Codex documentation:** Read [official-docs.md](references/official-docs.md) only when fetched official pages leave source selection, API schemas, or the requested implementation unresolved. This route is not manual-first.
- **Explicitly broad Codex setup, orientation, or cross-topic synthesis:** Read [codex-self-knowledge.md](references/codex-self-knowledge.md) when the eligible Codex manual or deeper Codex procedures are needed.

Read at most one primary reference. Do not open every route, bundled model guide, or helper script. Read a supporting reference or run a helper only when the chosen workflow demonstrably needs it.

## Source and execution boundaries

# Codex

> Capture Codex transcripts, file changes, tokens, and subagent sessions with Entire

The Codex integration uses Codex's project-level hook system.

Follow [Set Up an Agent](https://docs.entire.com/agents/setup.md) for shared installation, verification, and troubleshooting steps.

## Add Codex

```bash theme={null}
entire agent add codex
codex
```

Entire writes `.codex/hooks.json`. Codex enables hooks by default beginning with version 0.124.0, so Entire does not create `.codex/config.toml` or set `codex_hooks = true`.

The hooks capture session boundaries, prompts, completed turns, file-changing tool calls, and subagent events. Entire reads the full conversation and token usage from Codex rollout files under `~/.codex/` or `CODEX_HOME`.

## Limitations

Ephemeral Codex runs may not provide a transcript path. Entire can process their hook events, but it cannot attach a full transcript without the rollout file.

Entire records the subagents that changed files, materializes their transcripts into the parent's next checkpoint, and attributes their files to the parent session. It skips a subagent that wrote nothing, and it does not yet roll subagent tokens up into the parent session's totals.

## Resume and Import

`entire session resume BRANCH` restores the recorded session data when needed and prints:

```bash theme={null}
codex resume SESSION_ID
```

Entire can import existing Codex transcripts from the previous 30 days as read-only checkpoints.

See the [`session resume` command reference](https://docs.entire.com/cli-reference/session#session-resume) for flags and additional behavior.
