# Tareas con Git

La fuente oficial es main: [modelo Task](data_models/git-task.md).
El seguimiento no modifica el [contrato aprobado](contracts/task-model.md)
ni sustituye la [aprobacion de calidad](quality-approval.md).
La [integracion de KDD-Board](board-git.md) consume este mismo diario mediante
HTTP y WebMCP; los proyectos Git no guardan estados en JSON.

## Uso

Desde un repositorio Git con rama main, identidad de autor configurada y
arbol/indice limpios:

```text
python scripts/tasks.py create TASK-001 --title "Validar usuarios" --description "Cerrar validacion de usuarios" --contract knowledge/contracts/validate-user-record.md
python scripts/tasks.py ready TASK-001 --approved-ref SHA_COMPLETO_APROBADO
python scripts/tasks.py start TASK-001 --assignee equipo
python scripts/tasks.py block TASK-001 --reason "Falta decision de producto"
python scripts/tasks.py resume TASK-001 --reason "Decision registrada"
python scripts/tasks.py start TASK-001 --assignee equipo
python scripts/tasks.py list
python scripts/tasks.py show TASK-001
python scripts/tasks.py history TASK-001
```

create admite --depends-on TASK-NNN repetido. Las consultas admiten --json;
--repo-root DIR es una opcion global. No cambian el checkout. Un segundo
inicio tras resume reutiliza la rama, sin borrarla ni resetear sus commits.

El coordinador o humano cambia a task/TASK-001 para implementar y registrar
sus cambios. Despues integra esa rama en main con el flujo de revision del
proyecto. La CLI no realiza merge, push ni cambia protecciones de ramas.
Para preservar el recorrido original, integrar conservando los commits;
un squash no mantiene la relacion de ancestros exigida por finish.

Al publicar un diario completo mediante un PR, usar un merge que preserve los
commits originales. El validador audita tambien las transiciones importadas
desde su bifurcacion; el historial del tablero conserva sus SHA originales.
El merge debe copiar cada nodo importado sin modificarlo, y main no debe haber
cambiado ese mismo nodo desde la bifurcacion. Resolver ese conflicto requiere
reconciliar el diario con nuevas transiciones validas antes de volver a publicar.
No usar squash ni rebase para transportar cierres con evidencia ligada a SHA.

```text
python scripts/tasks.py finish TASK-001
python scripts/validate_tasks.py
python scripts/validate_tasks.py --base-ref SHA_INICIAL --head-ref main
```

finish usa el HEAD limpio actual como revision probada, ejecuta el oraculo
aprobado y crea un commit posterior de cierre. No acepta un PASS escrito a
mano. Los errores de pruebas no cambian el estado ni generan un cierre.
Las consultas leen blobs de main, incluso ejecutadas desde task/TASK-001.

## Operacion y limites

Las mutaciones serializan coordinadores con un lock local y rechazan cambios
ajenos en indice o checkout. Respetan los hooks de commit; un fallo anterior
a publicar el commit revierte solo los archivos propios de la operacion.
No coordinar simultaneamente con herramientas externas que ignoren ese lock.

Los commits locales deben publicarse por el flujo habitual para compartir
el estado. No reescribir el historial compartido; registrar nuevas decisiones.
Con main protegido, ejecutar el coordinador mediante el mecanismo autorizado
del proyecto: la CLI no evade la politica del servidor.

En Windows usar Git for Windows en el PATH; el Git MSYS de devkitPro devuelve
rutas POSIX y no es compatible con todas las verificaciones existentes.
El control de transiciones es un paso adicional, opt-in para proyectos
adoptantes; no cambia el conjunto fijo de 19 gates del despachador.

El runner de finish tiene un limite de 120 segundos y falla sin cerrar si
se agota. Para la suite completa de infraestructura de esta plantilla, CI
usa `validate_test_commands.py knowledge/contracts . --timeout 600`: el
contrato init-project ejecuta ademas una suite completa tras inicializar
una copia y puede superar el timeout predeterminado de 180 segundos en Windows.

## Contratos de implementacion

- [Modelo puro](contracts/task-model.md).
- [Diario y evidencia](contracts/task-journal.md).
- [Validador de historial](contracts/task-validation.md).
- [Publicacion mediante merge](contracts/task-publication.md).
- [CLI](contracts/task-cli.md).

context, docs, history, code-index records, and durable memories, then exposes
retrieval, verification, and evaluation surfaces for agents.

# Tareas con Git

La fuente oficial es main: [modelo Task](data_models/git-task.md).
El seguimiento no modifica el [contrato aprobado](contracts/task-model.md)
ni sustituye la [aprobacion de calidad](quality-approval.md).
La [integracion de KDD-Board](board-git.md) consume este mismo diario mediante
HTTP y WebMCP; los proyectos Git no guardan estados en JSON.

## Uso

Desde un repositorio Git con rama main, identidad de autor configurada y
arbol/indice limpios:

```text
python scripts/tasks.py create TASK-001 --title "Validar usuarios" --description "Cerrar validacion de usuarios" --contract knowledge/contracts/validate-user-record.md
python scripts/tasks.py ready TASK-001 --approved-ref SHA_COMPLETO_APROBADO
python scripts/tasks.py start TASK-001 --assignee equipo
python scripts/tasks.py block TASK-001 --reason "Falta decision de producto"
python scripts/tasks.py resume TASK-001 --reason "Decision registrada"
python scripts/tasks.py start TASK-001 --assignee equipo
python scripts/tasks.py list
python scripts/tasks.py show TASK-001
python scripts/tasks.py history TASK-001
```

create admite --depends-on TASK-NNN repetido. Las consultas admiten --json;
--repo-root DIR es una opcion global. No cambian el checkout. Un segundo
inicio tras resume reutiliza la rama, sin borrarla ni resetear sus commits.

El coordinador o humano cambia a task/TASK-001 para implementar y registrar
sus cambios. Despues integra esa rama en main con el flujo de revision del
proyecto. La CLI no realiza merge, push ni cambia protecciones de ramas.
Para preservar el recorrido original, integrar conservando los commits;
un squash no mantiene la relacion de ancestros exigida por finish.

Al publicar un diario completo mediante un PR, usar un merge que preserve los
commits originales. El validador audita tambien las transiciones importadas
desde su bifurcacion; el historial del tablero conserva sus SHA originales.
El merge debe copiar cada nodo importado sin modificarlo, y main no debe haber
cambiado ese mismo nodo desde la bifurcacion. Resolver ese conflicto requiere
reconciliar el diario con nuevas transiciones validas antes de volver a publicar.
No usar squash ni rebase para transportar cierres con evidencia ligada a SHA.

```text
python scripts/tasks.py finish TASK-001
python scripts/validate_tasks.py
python scripts/validate_tasks.py --base-ref SHA_INICIAL --head-ref main
```

finish usa el HEAD limpio actual como revision probada, ejecuta el oraculo
aprobado y crea un commit posterior de cierre. No acepta un PASS escrito a
mano. Los errores de pruebas no cambian el estado ni generan un cierre.
Las consultas leen blobs de main, incluso ejecutadas desde task/TASK-001.

## Operacion y limites

Las mutaciones serializan coordinadores con un lock local y rechazan cambios
ajenos en indice o checkout. Respetan los hooks de commit; un fallo anterior
a publicar el commit revierte solo los archivos propios de la operacion.
No coordinar simultaneamente con herramientas externas que ignoren ese lock.

Los commits locales deben publicarse por el flujo habitual para compartir
el estado. No reescribir el historial compartido; registrar nuevas decisiones.
Con main protegido, ejecutar el coordinador mediante el mecanismo autorizado
del proyecto: la CLI no evade la politica del servidor.

En Windows usar Git for Windows en el PATH; el Git MSYS de devkitPro devuelve
rutas POSIX y no es compatible con todas las verificaciones existentes.
El control de transiciones es un paso adicional, opt-in para proyectos
adoptantes; no cambia el conjunto fijo de 19 gates del despachador.

El runner de finish tiene un limite de 120 segundos y falla sin cerrar si
se agota. Para la suite completa de infraestructura de esta plantilla, CI
usa `validate_test_commands.py knowledge/contracts . --timeout 600`: el
contrato init-project ejecuta ademas una suite completa tras inicializar
una copia y puede superar el timeout predeterminado de 180 segundos en Windows.

- [Validador de historial](contracts/task-validation.md).
- [Publicacion mediante merge](contracts/task-publication.md).
- [CLI](contracts/task-cli.md).

Find the code for a task from a plain-language query (start here)

Usage:
  entire graph query --query "issue or concept" --repo . [--top-k 10] [--format text|json|ndjson|agent] [--head] [--profile fast|full] [--deep]
  entire graph query [flags] "issue or concept"

Ranked source regions for a plain-language description, with source and file:line inline, budgeted to drop straight into context. This is the first move for almost every locate task.

By default query returns: ranked candidate fix sites (top hits as full function bodies), RELATED SITES, the COVERING TEST plus other tests over the same code (ALSO COVERING), SAME-CONCEPT LITERAL (every place the concept is named, tagged EDIT/CONSUMER/DOC), a VERIFY line (the narrowest test command for the file), and a CLOSED-SET WARNING when a switch over a sealed set would fail at runtime. The three reference blocks (container map, signature types, declaration card) are OFF by default because they cost turns in agent sessions; --reference-blocks all turns them on for interactive reading.

--verify-block off (or --omit-verify, or ENTIRE_GRAPH_VERIFY_BLOCK=off) removes the VERIFY block and nothing else: the test command and the run-once/fix/stop advice that rides with it. That advice would help an agent with no tool just as much, so it exists for fair A/B comparisons (both arms get it, or neither). JSON then omits verify_command and reports stats.verify_omitted. In agent format the freed bytes go to ranked results under the same --max-context-bytes, so off is a different selection, not the on payload with lines deleted.

--top-k caps normal results, including automatic related sites and covering tests, without changing retrieval strategy. Explicit --callee-hop may add called-helper results beyond that cap, under its existing byte-budget and ranked-source protections. --deep additionally runs the exhaustive sparse (BM25) pass and fuses it with the semantic ranking (slower, reads every eligible file).

Ranking returns one region per unit, which is right for code and wrong for whole prose documents: one markdown document can hold the answer across several distant regions. So for prose the unit is the SECTION, not the file — a document's headed sections are ranked against every other section on their own scores, exactly as independent files would be (--document-resolution ranks a document as one unit instead). Separately, and on prose of any shape including headed documents, when fewer distinct units match than --top-k asked for, the spare slots are spent returning finer regions of the same document as results of their own (multi-resolution retrieval) — strictly additive, so it never displaces a unit and never breaches --max-context-bytes. --single-resolution turns that off. The two stack: a headed document can be ranked by section AND have spare slots filled with promoted passages, so a prose payload may carry both.

Flags:
  --query <text>            The task or bug in one plain sentence; alternatively supply one final argument
  --repo <path>             Repository to search (default: current repo)
  --top-k <n>               Maximum normal results, including related/covering entries (--callee-hop may add helpers) (default: 10)
  --format text|json|ndjson|agent
                            Output format; text is tiered for reading, agent is compact (default: json)
  --head                    Search the committed tree (cached) instead of the working tree
  --profile syntax-only|fast|full
                            Parsing depth; use full for bug-fix/locate (call-graph active) (default: fast)
  --deep                    Also run the exhaustive BM25 pass and fuse it (slower)
  --callee-hop              Add called-helper results beyond --top-k, subject to byte-budget and ranked-source protections
  --single-resolution       One result per ranked unit; do not spend spare slots on finer regions of a prose document
  --document-resolution     Rank a prose document as one unit; do not rank its sections separately
  --max-context-bytes <n>   Output byte budget; 0 = unbounded. Unset with --format agent: the smallest of 4096/8192/16384 that shows the top hit whole, else 24576 (default: 24576)
  --reference-blocks all|container-map,signature-types,type-card
                            Turn reference blocks back on (off by default)
  --verify-block on|off     off removes the VERIFY block (suggested test command plus its run/fix/stop advice) in every format; exists for fair A/B comparisons against an arm with no tool. Env: ENTIRE_GRAPH_VERIFY_BLOCK (default: on)
  --omit-verify             Shorthand for --verify-block off
  --max-indexed-files <n>   Bound cold-search parsing to N files
  --index-all-files         Widen cold-search parsing to every file
  --cache-dir <path>        Override the committed-tree cache directory
  --no-cache                Disable the committed-tree cache

Examples:
  entire graph query --repo . --format text "token refresh returns 401"
  entire graph query --repo . --query "token refresh returns 401" --format text --top-k 8
  entire graph query --repo . --query "csv export ordering" --profile full
Task-relevant symbols, relations, and test suggestions from the committed-tree store (JSON)

Usage:
  entire graph context --repo . --task "<task text>" [--limit N] [--tests-limit N] [--relations-limit N] [--allow-ancestor N] [--profile full] [--cache-dir path] [--ignore-file path] [--include-file path]

The delegation surface for downstream consumers such as Entire Brain's brief: task text in, the store's ranked task-relevant symbols plus their relation fan-out and test suggestions out, as one JSON document. It reads ONLY the committed tree's sqlite store sidecar — it never parses and never builds — so latency is bounded by indexed reads (measured ~0.5s on a 52k-symbol repository).

The store sidecar exists when the cache variant was built with ENTIRE_GRAPH_SEARCH_STORE=1 (`entire graph index --head`). Without one (or with a stale one), the response carries store_unavailable=true with empty lists, so a consumer degrades exactly as it would with the plugin absent instead of paying a parse.

--allow-ancestor N (opt-in, at most 5) answers an exact miss from the newest of the N nearest first-parent ancestors that has a store under the same provider version and ignore policy, provided the paths changed since then are known completely and number at most 5% of its indexed files. Every symbol, test and relation in a changed file is withheld, and the response carries a typed stale block (ancestor_commit, ancestor_tree, commits_behind, changed_files, excluded_records). Without the block the answer is exact. A refused ancestor returns the exact miss unchanged. `graph store` never serves an ancestor.

Flags:
  --repo <path>           Repository (default: current repo)
  --ignore-file <path>    Additional ignore file; repeatable, must match the indexed policy
  --include-file <path>   Additional include file; repeatable, must match the indexed policy
  --task <text>           Task text to find context for (required)
  --limit <N>             Maximum symbols returned (default: 12)
  --tests-limit <N>       Maximum test suggestions returned (default: 6)
  --relations-limit <N>   Maximum relations returned; highest confidence kept, relations_truncated signals a cut (default: 200)
  --allow-ancestor <N>    On an exact miss, serve a first-parent ancestor's store up to N (max 5) commits back, changed files withheld, marked by a stale block (default: 0)
  --profile syntax-only|fast|full
                          Indexing profile of the store to read (match the index that built it) (default: full)
  --cache-dir <path>      Cache directory holding the store (default: plugin data dir, else user cache dir)

Examples:
  entire graph context --repo . --task "add a kind filter flag to the recall command"
One-shot blast radius for changing a symbol

Usage:
  entire graph impact --symbol NAME|<file>:<line> --repo . [--depth 1|2] [--limit 15] [--format text|json]

Everything the graph knows about changing one symbol in a single bounded explanation: direct + transitive callers (depth <=2), callees, type consumers (USES_TYPE/PARAM_TYPE/RETURNS_TYPE), data flows, files that historically co-change with the symbol's file, and same-container siblings. Run this before changing a function/type's behavior.

Ambiguous names return the definition list; rerun with --file/--line/--kind (or --symbol <file>:<line>) to pick one.

Flags:
  --symbol NAME|<file>:<line>
                            Symbol to analyze (required)
  --repo <path>             Repository (default: current repo)
  --file <path>             Disambiguate an ambiguous name by file
  --line <n>                Disambiguate by line
  --kind <kind>             Disambiguate by symbol kind
  --depth 1|2               Caller-traversal depth (default: 2)
  --limit <n>               Max entries per section (default: 15)
  --format text|json        Output format
  --max-context-bytes <n>   Total text budget (default: 4096)
  --exclude-tests           Drop test-only entries
  --head                    Query the committed tree (cached)
  --profile syntax-only|fast|full
                            Parsing depth (default: full)

Examples:
  entire graph impact --repo . --symbol WriteText
Summarize recorded sources, freshness, background activity, and live workspace state without scanning index contents. Use doctor for deep integrity checks.

Usage:
  entire-brain status [path] [flags]

Flags:
      --details          Include staged, unstaged, and untracked file classifications (does not audit index contents)
      --fail-on string   Return nonzero after emitting the report when the selected gate trips: release, unsafe, degraded, blind-spots, none (default "none")
  -h, --help             help for status
      --json             Emit machine-readable JSON
      --verbose          Print the full report (coverage, freshness axes, blind spots, live state) instead of the short summary
Search the brain (BM25 lexical ranking). Supply the text positionally or with --query. Flags may appear before or after the text.

Usage:
  entire-brain query [query] [flags]

Flags:
      --after string               Conversation source only: sessions at or after this time (RFC3339 or YYYY-MM-DD)
      --agent string               Conversation source only: exchanges captured by this agent/harness (e.g. "Claude Code", "Codex")
      --before string              Conversation source only: sessions before this time (RFC3339 or YYYY-MM-DD)
      --branch string              Branch for memories (default: current); with --source conversation also filters exchanges to that captured branch
      --concept stringArray        Conversation source only: additional concept (repeatable, up to 4); sessions must match the query AND every concept
      --format string              Output format: json or cli (QMD-style alias for --json)
  -h, --help                       help for query
      --include-abstract           Conversation source only: include bounded evidence-linked session previews (never affects ranking)
      --json                       Emit machine-readable JSON
      --keyword                    Match keywords and identifiers only

Ranked source regions for a plain-language description, with source and file:line inline, budgeted to drop straight into context. This is the first move for almost every locate task.

By default query returns: ranked candidate fix sites (top hits as full function bodies), RELATED SITES, the COVERING TEST plus other tests over the same code (ALSO COVERING), SAME-CONCEPT LITERAL (every place the concept is named, tagged EDIT/CONSUMER/DOC), a VERIFY line (the narrowest test command for the file), and a CLOSED-SET WARNING when a switch over a sealed set would fail at runtime. The three reference blocks (container map, signature types, declaration card) are OFF by default because they cost turns in agent sessions; --reference-blocks all turns them on for interactive reading.

--verify-block off (or --omit-verify, or ENTIRE_GRAPH_VERIFY_BLOCK=off) removes the VERIFY block and nothing else: the test command and the run-once/fix/stop advice that rides with it. That advice would help an agent with no tool just as much, so it exists for fair A/B comparisons (both arms get it, or neither). JSON then omits verify_command and reports stats.verify_omitted. In agent format the freed bytes go to ranked results under the same --max-context-bytes, so off is a different selection, not the on payload with lines deleted.

--top-k caps normal results, including automatic related sites and covering tests, without changing retrieval strategy. Explicit --callee-hop may add called-helper results beyond that cap, under its existing byte-budget and ranked-source protections. --deep additionally runs the exhaustive sparse (BM25) pass and fuses it with the semantic ranking (slower, reads every eligible file).

Ranking returns one region per unit, which is right for code and wrong for whole prose documents: one markdown document can hold the answer across several distant regions. So for prose the unit is the SECTION, not the file — a document's headed sections are ranked against every other section on their own scores, exactly as independent files would be (--document-resolution ranks a document as one unit instead). Separately, and on prose of any shape including headed documents, when fewer distinct units match than --top-k asked for, the spare slots are spent returning finer regions of the same document as results of their own (multi-resolution retrieval) — strictly additive, so it never displaces a unit and never breaches --max-context-bytes. --single-resolution turns that off. Task-relevant symbols, relations, and test suggestions from the committed-tree store (JSON)

Usage:

The delegation surface for downstream consumers such as Entire Brain's brief: task text in, the store's ranked task-relevant symbols plus their relation fan-out and test suggestions out, as one JSON document. It reads ONLY the committed tree's sqlite store sidecar — it never parses and never builds — so latency is bounded by indexed reads (measured ~0.5s on a 52k-symbol repository).

The store sidecar exists when the cache variant was built with ENTIRE_GRAPH_SEARCH_STORE=1 (`entire graph index --head`). Without one (or with a stale one), the response carries store_unavailable=true with empty lists, so a consumer degrades exactly as it would with the plugin absent instead of paying a parse.

--allow-ancestor N (opt-in, at most 5) answers an exact miss from the newest of the N nearest first-parent ancestors that has a store under the same provider version and ignore policy, provided the paths changed since then are known completely and number at most 5% of its indexed files. Every symbol, test and relation in a changed file is withheld, and the response carries a typed stale block (ancestor_commit, ancestor_tree, commits_behind, changed_files, excluded_records). Without the block the answer is exact. A refused ancestor returns the exact miss unchanged. `graph store` never serves an ancestor.

# How entire-graph Works

> Understand how entire-graph analyzes a repository, guides your coding agent, and works with Search.

Once entire-graph is [installed and enabled for a repository](https://docs.entire.com/guides/graph/set-up-graph.md), your coding agent can use it to investigate the codebase during a task. entire-graph analyzes the repository locally and returns relevant files, symbols, and relationships. Your agent then inspects the source before answering a question or making changes.

## What entire-graph Analyzes

entire-graph maps files, symbols, and relationships such as callers, callees, and type usage. It also uses a limited amount of Git history to identify files that often change together.

entire-graph runs locally and does not send your code to a model or external service. It can reuse a local cache to make later queries faster.

## When to Use entire-graph or Search

entire-graph and [Search](https://docs.entire.com/guides/search/overview.md) can both help your agent find code, but they serve different purposes.

| | entire-graph | Search |
| - | - | - |
| Find code | Finds and ranks relevant code in the current repository | Finds matching code across indexed repositories |
| Understand relationships | Traces callers, callees, type usage, and potential impact | Returns code locations without tracing their relationships |
| Find past context | Uses limited Git history to identify related code | Finds previous commits, sessions, and agent work |
| Where it runs | Runs locally without sending your code elsewhere | Uses Entire's online search and requires an internet connection |
| Best used for | Understanding how code connects before making a change | Locating code or learning the history behind it |

The two can work together. Your agent might use Search to locate code or find previous work, then use entire-graph to trace how that code connects and what a change could affect.

## What entire-graph Might Not Find

How deeply entire-graph can analyze your code depends on the language, and coverage comes in two tiers.

**Semantic languages** are parsed for relationships, so `impact`, `neighbors`, and `def` can trace callers, callees, and type usage. There are 36:

Bash, C, C#, C++, CUE, Clojure, ClojureScript, Dart, Elixir, Erlang, F#, Go, Groovy, HCL, Haskell, Java, JavaScript, Julia, Kotlin, Lua, OCaml, Objective-C, PHP, Perl, Protocol Buffers, Python, R, Ruby, Rust, SQL, Scala, Swift, TypeScript, YAML, Zig, Zsh

**Inventory-only languages** are recognized for file and symbol structure without call or type analysis. There are 149 of these, which is why a file can appear in `query` results while `neighbors` returns no relationships for the symbols inside it.

> [!NOTE]
>
> These counts describe the current release. Run `entire graph capabilities --json` to see what your installed build supports, and read `semantic_languages` for the tier that traces relationships.

Because entire-graph analyzes source without running it, it may miss connections created dynamically through interfaces, reflection, generated code, or other runtime behavior. Treat its results as a focused starting point and verify them against the source.

## Continue With

> **[Use entire-graph with Your Coding Agent](https://docs.entire.com/guides/graph/use-graph.md)**
>
> Learn what to ask and what happens after you prompt your agent.

> **[Install and Enable entire-graph](https://docs.entire.com/guides/graph/set-up-graph.md)**
>
> Install entire-graph and add its instructions to a repository.

> **[entire-graph CLI Reference](https://docs.entire.com/cli-reference/graph.md)**
>
> Review entire-graph commands and options.

How deeply entire-graph can analyze your code depends on the language, and coverage comes in two tiers.

**Semantic languages** are parsed for relationships, so `impact`, `neighbors`, and `def` can trace callers, callees, and type usage. There are 36:

Bash, C, C#, C++, CUE, Clojure, ClojureScript, Dart, Elixir, Erlang, F#, Go, Groovy, HCL, Haskell, Java, JavaScript, Julia, Kotlin, Lua, OCaml, Objective-C, PHP, Perl, Protocol Buffers, Python, R, Ruby, Rust, SQL, Scala, Swift, TypeScript, YAML, Zig, Zsh

**Inventory-only languages** are recognized for file and symbol structure without call or type analysis. There are 149 of these, which is why a file can appear in `query` results while `neighbors` returns no relationships for the symbols inside it.

> [!NOTE]
>
> These counts describe the current release. Run `entire graph capabilities --json` to see what your installed build supports, and read `semantic_languages` for the tier that traces relationships.

Because entire-graph analyzes source without running it, it may miss connections created dynamically through interfaces, reflection, generated code, or other runtime behavior. Treat its results as a focused starting point and verify them against the source.

# Getting started with Brain

> Learn what you can do with Brain and find the right command for each task.

You can use Brain to find earlier decisions, save lessons, and give your agent context before it starts work. Below are some ways to use Brain in your project.

[Install Brain and set up your repository](https://docs.entire.com/guides/brain/overview.md#before-you-start) first. Run these commands from the repository, and replace the example questions and rules with your own.

## Get to Know a Project

If you are joining a project or returning after a break, you can ask Brain for an overview of its structure, tools, and conventions.

```bash theme={null}
entire brain overview
```

## Get Context Before Starting a Task

Describe what you want to build or change. Brain gathers relevant memories, earlier work, code locations, and possible tests into a brief.

```bash theme={null}
entire brain brief "add rate limiting to the upload endpoint"
```

You can now use the brief to plan your work or give your coding agent a starting point. Code locations in the brief come from entire-graph.

## Find Out Why a Decision Was Made

Search earlier work before reopening a decision or trying an approach your team has already explored.

```bash theme={null}
entire brain query "why did we remove the queue abstraction"
```

This helps you read the supporting sources to understand the decision and whether it still applies.

## Search for a Topic

Search for a topic by the words you expect to appear in saved memories, history, or docs:

```bash theme={null}
entire brain query "rate limiter"
```

`query` ranks results by keyword relevance using BM25, so results match the words in your query rather than their meaning. If a search returns nothing useful, try the terms your team would have used when the decision was recorded.

The `--semantic` flag is deprecated and has no effect. It is still accepted as an alias so existing scripts keep working, but it returns the same keyword-ranked results.

To narrow the search to one kind of source, use `--source` with `fact`, `history`, or `doc`:

```bash theme={null}
entire brain query "rate limiter" --source fact
```

To rank recent results higher, add `--recency`. You can change how quickly older results lose weight with `--recency-half-life`, which defaults to `2160h` (90 days):

```bash theme={null}
entire brain query "rate limiter" --recency --recency-half-life 720h
```

## Save a Rule for Future Work

You can also record a decision or lesson as a memory so another session can find it. Only save rules that are true for your project.

```bash theme={null}
entire brain remember "Retry failed requests at most three times." --path constraints.retry.policy
```

The path flag groups the memory under a topic. This lets you save the memory without asking an agent to choose a category.

## Save a Rule for Every Repository

Some memories, such as a personal preference or a team convention, apply to every repository you work in. Record them globally:

```bash theme={null}
entire brain remember "The staging cluster is in eu-west-1." --global
```

Brain recalls global memories from every repository and labels them `(global)` in results. To list them:

```bash theme={null}
entire brain memories global
```

To leave global memories out of a search, add `--no-global` to `query` or `recall`.

## Look Up Saved Rules

Before changing behavior, you can check what your project has already recorded about it.

```bash theme={null}
entire brain recall "retry policy"
```

Use `recall` for saved memories and `query` for a broader search across memories, history, and docs.

## Review Memories as Markdown Files

Write your memories out as one Markdown file per memory, so you can read, search, and diff them with your usual tools:

```bash theme={null}
entire brain memories files --dir brain-memories
```

The files are a copy. Brain rewrites the directory on each run and does not read the files back, so use `remember` and `memories retract` to change memories.

## Import Memories from Another Tool

If you have memories in mem0, import its export file. Preview the import first:

```bash theme={null}
entire brain memories import --file mem0-export.json --dry-run
entire brain memories import --file mem0-export.json
```

Imported memories are filed under `project.imported` by default. Change this with `--path-prefix`.

## Search Documents That Are Not Code

Brain reads PDF, Word, Excel, and PowerPoint files under `docs/` along with Markdown, so they come back from `query` and `brief`. Extraction runs locally, with no model or network calls.

To check what Brain reads from a file:

```bash theme={null}
entire brain docs extract docs/spec.pdf
```

Scanned PDFs have no text layer, so Brain reports them instead of indexing an empty document.

## Check What a Code Change Could Affect

With entire-graph installed, inspect the impact of changing a function or type. Replace `ValidateToken` with a symbol from your code.

```bash theme={null}
entire brain inspect impact ValidateToken
```

You can also inspect changes since the last index:

```bash theme={null}
entire brain inspect changes
```

## Notify Another Service When Memory Changes

Brain can send a JSON event to an HTTP endpoint when a memory is recorded or retracted, or when memory is refreshed. This lets a CI job, chat channel, or index react without polling.

```bash theme={null}
export ENTIRE_BRAIN_WEBHOOK_URL=https://hooks.example.com/entire
export REDACTED brain webhook test
```

| Variable | What it does |
| - | - |
| `ENTIRE_BRAIN_WEBHOOK_URL` | Endpoint to send events to. Webhooks are off when it is unset. |
| `ENTIRE_BRAIN_WEBHOOK_SECRET` | Signs each request with HMAC-SHA256 in the `X-Entire-Signature-256` header. |
| `ENTIRE_BRAIN_WEBHOOK_INCLUDE_TEXT` | Set to `1` to include memory text in events. Text is left out by default. |
| `ENTIRE_BRAIN_NO_EGRESS` | Turns off all webhooks, along with other network calls. |

Run `entire brain webhook events` to list the events Brain sends.

## Check Whether Memory Is Current

You can see which sources are available, missing, or out of date, using:

```bash theme={null}
entire brain status --verbose
```

If something needs attention, `doctor` prints the command that fixes it:

```bash theme={null}
entire brain doctor
```

Check whether saved memories still point to matching sources:

```bash theme={null}
entire brain verify
```

A memory entered by hand can show `unverifiable-here` because it has no source reference. Verification checks references, not whether a memory is correct.

# Getting started with Brain

> Learn what you can do with Brain and find the right command for each task.

You can use Brain to find earlier decisions, save lessons, and give your agent context before it starts work. Below are some ways to use Brain in your project.

[Install Brain and set up your repository](https://docs.entire.com/guides/brain/overview.md#before-you-start) first. Run these commands from the repository, and replace the example questions and rules with your own.

## Get to Know a Project

If you are joining a project or returning after a break, you can ask Brain for an overview of its structure, tools, and conventions.

```bash theme={null}
entire brain overview
```

## Get Context Before Starting a Task

Describe what you want to build or change. Brain gathers relevant memories, earlier work, code locations, and possible tests into a brief.

```bash theme={null}
entire brain brief "add rate limiting to the upload endpoint"
```

You can now use the brief to plan your work or give your coding agent a starting point. Code locations in the brief come from entire-graph.

## Find Out Why a Decision Was Made

Search earlier work before reopening a decision or trying an approach your team has already explored.

```bash theme={null}
entire brain query "why did we remove the queue abstraction"
```

This helps you read the supporting sources to understand the decision and whether it still applies.

## Search for a Topic

Search for a topic by the words you expect to appear in saved memories, history, or docs:

```bash theme={null}
entire brain query "rate limiter"
```

`query` ranks results by keyword relevance using BM25, so results match the words in your query rather than their meaning. If a search returns nothing useful, try the terms your team would have used when the decision was recorded.

The `--semantic` flag is deprecated and has no effect. It is still accepted as an alias so existing scripts keep working, but it returns the same keyword-ranked results.

To narrow the search to one kind of source, use `--source` with `fact`, `history`, or `doc`:

```bash theme={null}
entire brain query "rate limiter" --source fact
```

To rank recent results higher, add `--recency`. You can change how quickly older results lose weight with `--recency-half-life`, which defaults to `2160h` (90 days):

```bash theme={null}
entire brain query "rate limiter" --recency --recency-half-life 720h
```

## Save a Rule for Future Work

You can also record a decision or lesson as a memory so another session can find it. Only save rules that are true for your project.

```bash theme={null}
entire brain remember "Retry failed requests at most three times." --path constraints.retry.policy
```

The path flag groups the memory under a topic. This lets you save the memory without asking an agent to choose a category.

## Save a Rule for Every Repository

Some memories, such as a personal preference or a team convention, apply to every repository you work in. Record them globally:

```bash theme={null}
entire brain remember "The staging cluster is in eu-west-1." --global
```

Brain recalls global memories from every repository and labels them `(global)` in results. To list them:

```bash theme={null}
entire brain memories global
```

To leave global memories out of a search, add `--no-global` to `query` or `recall`.

## Look Up Saved Rules

Before changing behavior, you can check what your project has already recorded about it.

```bash theme={null}
entire brain recall "retry policy"
```

Use `recall` for saved memories and `query` for a broader search across memories, history, and docs.

## Review Memories as Markdown Files

Write your memories out as one Markdown file per memory, so you can read, search, and diff them with your usual tools:

```bash theme={null}
entire brain memories files --dir brain-memories
```

The files are a copy. Brain rewrites the directory on each run and does not read the files back, so use `remember` and `memories retract` to change memories.

## Import Memories from Another Tool

If you have memories in mem0, import its export file. Preview the import first:

```bash theme={null}
entire brain memories import --file mem0-export.json --dry-run
entire brain memories import --file mem0-export.json
```

Imported memories are filed under `project.imported` by default. Change this with `--path-prefix`.

## Search Documents That Are Not Code

Brain reads PDF, Word, Excel, and PowerPoint files under `docs/` along with Markdown, so they come back from `query` and `brief`. Extraction runs locally, with no model or network calls.

To check what Brain reads from a file:

```bash theme={null}
entire brain docs extract docs/spec.pdf
```

Scanned PDFs have no text layer, so Brain reports them instead of indexing an empty document.

## Check What a Code Change Could Affect

With entire-graph installed, inspect the impact of changing a function or type. Replace `ValidateToken` with a symbol from your code.

```bash theme={null}
entire brain inspect impact ValidateToken
```

You can also inspect changes since the last index:

```bash theme={null}
entire brain inspect changes
```

## Notify Another Service When Memory Changes

Brain can send a JSON event to an HTTP endpoint when a memory is recorded or retracted, or when memory is refreshed. This lets a CI job, chat channel, or index react without polling.

```bash theme={null}
export ENTIRE_BRAIN_WEBHOOK_URL=https://hooks.example.com/entire
export REDACTED brain webhook test
```

| Variable | What it does |
| - | - |
| `ENTIRE_BRAIN_WEBHOOK_URL` | Endpoint to send events to. Webhooks are off when it is unset. |
| `ENTIRE_BRAIN_WEBHOOK_SECRET` | Signs each request with HMAC-SHA256 in the `X-Entire-Signature-256` header. |
| `ENTIRE_BRAIN_WEBHOOK_INCLUDE_TEXT` | Set to `1` to include memory text in events. Text is left out by default. |
| `ENTIRE_BRAIN_NO_EGRESS` | Turns off all webhooks, along with other network calls. |

Run `entire brain webhook events` to list the events Brain sends.

## Check Whether Memory Is Current

You can see which sources are available, missing, or out of date, using:

```bash theme={null}
entire brain status --verbose
```

If something needs attention, `doctor` prints the command that fixes it:

```bash theme={null}
entire brain doctor
```

Check whether saved memories still point to matching sources:

```bash theme={null}
entire brain verify
```

A memory entered by hand can show `unverifiable-here` because it has no source reference. Verification checks references, not whether a memory is correct.

# How entire-graph Works

> Understand how entire-graph analyzes a repository, guides your coding agent, and works with Search.

Once entire-graph is [installed and enabled for a repository](https://docs.entire.com/guides/graph/set-up-graph.md), your coding agent can use it to investigate the codebase during a task. entire-graph analyzes the repository locally and returns relevant files, symbols, and relationships. Your agent then inspects the source before answering a question or making changes.

## What entire-graph Analyzes

entire-graph maps files, symbols, and relationships such as callers, callees, and type usage. It also uses a limited amount of Git history to identify files that often change together.

entire-graph runs locally and does not send your code to a model or external service. It can reuse a local cache to make later queries faster.

## When to Use entire-graph or Search

entire-graph and [Search](https://docs.entire.com/guides/search/overview.md) can both help your agent find code, but they serve different purposes.

| | entire-graph | Search |
| - | - | - |
| Find code | Finds and ranks relevant code in the current repository | Finds matching code across indexed repositories |
| Understand relationships | Traces callers, callees, type usage, and potential impact | Returns code locations without tracing their relationships |
| Find past context | Uses limited Git history to identify related code | Finds previous commits, sessions, and agent work |
| Where it runs | Runs locally without sending your code elsewhere | Uses Entire's online search and requires an internet connection |
| Best used for | Understanding how code connects before making a change | Locating code or learning the history behind it |

The two can work together. Your agent might use Search to locate code or find previous work, then use entire-graph to trace how that code connects and what a change could affect.

## What entire-graph Might Not Find

How deeply entire-graph can analyze your code depends on the language, and coverage comes in two tiers.

**Semantic languages** are parsed for relationships, so `impact`, `neighbors`, and `def` can trace callers, callees, and type usage. There are 36:

Bash, C, C#, C++, CUE, Clojure, ClojureScript, Dart, Elixir, Erlang, F#, Go, Groovy, HCL, Haskell, Java, JavaScript, Julia, Kotlin, Lua, OCaml, Objective-C, PHP, Perl, Protocol Buffers, Python, R, Ruby, Rust, SQL, Scala, Swift, TypeScript, YAML, Zig, Zsh

**Inventory-only languages** are recognized for file and symbol structure without call or type analysis. There are 149 of these, which is why a file can appear in `query` results while `neighbors` returns no relationships for the symbols inside it.

> [!NOTE]
>
> These counts describe the current release. Run `entire graph capabilities --json` to see what your installed build supports, and read `semantic_languages` for the tier that traces relationships.

Because entire-graph analyzes source without running it, it may miss connections created dynamically through interfaces, reflection, generated code, or other runtime behavior. Treat its results as a focused starting point and verify them against the source.

## Continue With

> **[Use entire-graph with Your Coding Agent](https://docs.entire.com/guides/graph/use-graph.md)**
>
> Learn what to ask and what happens after you prompt your agent.

> **[Install and Enable entire-graph](https://docs.entire.com/guides/graph/set-up-graph.md)**
>

> **[entire-graph CLI Reference](https://docs.entire.com/cli-reference/graph.md)**

**Sí: Entire puede aportar mejoras concretas a KDD, especialmente en trazabilidad y análisis de impacto.** Ya hice pruebas sobre este repositorio mientras avanzaba la otra sesión.

Confirmé que la nueva sesión de Codex está siendo capturada. Hay trabajo pendiente registrado, aunque todavía **cero checkpoints consolidados en commits**.

Estas son las mejoras que priorizaría:

| Prioridad | Mejora para KDD | Aplicación |
|---|---|---|
| Alta | Explicar cómo se produjo un cambio | Asociar tarea, contrato, commit y checkpoint para consultar prompts y decisiones durante la revisión. |
| Alta | Analizar el impacto antes de editar | Usar Graph para localizar llamadas, dependencias y posibles pruebas afectadas. |
| Media | Mejorar la selección de contexto | Usar los resultados de Graph como entrada auxiliar al ensamblador de KDD, conservando presupuesto, hashes y guardrails. |
| Posterior | Recuperar aprendizajes entre sesiones | Incorporar Brain cuando exista suficiente historial y se compruebe la vigencia de sus recuerdos. |

**Graph mostró utilidad real, con límites.** Identificó correctamente la cadena `_retrieve_okf_nodes → _assemble_okf_nodes → assemble`. En tres consultas iniciales en español encontró el archivo esperado dentro de los cinco primeros resultados en una ocasión. Dos consultas reformuladas en inglés, con análisis ampliado, localizaron ambos archivos esperados. Las consultas originales siguieron fallando al ampliar el análisis: conviene verificar sus resultados contra el código.

También encontré una oportunidad en KDD: su [selector actual de contexto](D:/Repo/kdd_2/scripts/assemble_context.py:323) puntúa nombres y etiquetas. Una consulta sobre cierre de tareas terminó usando el fallback de los 197 nodos disponibles. Eso justifica evaluar una recuperación más precisa.

**Brain requiere más preparación.** Estaba instalado, pero sin índice del repositorio; además, su servicio automático de actualización todavía no soporta Windows. Su búsqueda actual utiliza BM25, basado en palabras clave. [Documentación de Brain](https://docs.entire.com/guides/brain/quickstart.md)

Mi recomendación es incorporar **checkpoints y Graph como ayudas opcionales**, manteniendo los contratos, oráculos aprobados y validadores de KDD como criterios de aceptación. La siguiente evaluación debería medir tiempo de investigación, archivos relevantes recuperados y tokens consumidos en tareas comparables. El ahorro de tokens en KDD todavía está por demostrar.

# Reglas para Agentes de IA

Si eres un agente de IA interactuando con este repositorio, debes acatar las siguientes reglas:

1. **Metodología KDD Obligatoria**: Este repositorio utiliza Knowledge-Driven Development. Antes de escribir código, debes leer los contratos en `knowledge/contracts/` y la spec normativa de los nodos OKF en `knowledge/OKF-SPEC.md`.
2. **Carga la Skill Local**: Tienes disponible la skill `kdd-okf-ccdd-hybrid` en el directorio `.agents/skills/`. Debes adoptarla en tu contexto para entender cómo generar y validar los contratos híbridos OKF-CCDD.
3. **No dupliques contexto**: Utiliza enlaces de markdown relativos a `knowledge/` cuando necesites explicar el porqué de una implementación.
4. **Validación Determinista (dos niveles)**: la referencia canónica completa (niveles, gate multi-lenguaje, export, `tc-tests-frozen`) está en [knowledge/validacion.md](../knowledge/validacion.md) — léela antes de validar; esta regla no la duplica. Resumen: nivel 1 (obligatorio) = `python scripts/validate_contracts.py knowledge/contracts` (incluye el sello obligatorio `tests_sha256` del oráculo; sellar con `--hash`) + `python scripts/validate_specs.py specs` + `python scripts/validate_okf.py knowledge` (estructura/frontmatter de nodos OKF) + `python scripts/lint_ascii.py scripts` + `python scripts/validate_rules.py <dir>` (rule contracts, capa opcional) + `python scripts/validate_skills.py skills .agents/skills` (skills de agente, capa opcional) + `python scripts/validate_changelog.py` (coherencia CHANGELOG↔reportes, capa opcional) + `python scripts/validate_ux_page.py examples/ux-page` (UX/accesibilidad mecánica sobre paginas HTML autocontenidas, capa opcional) + `python scripts/validate_diagrams.py <dir>` (diagramas Mermaid flowchart verificados contra un .diagram-contract.json declarativo, capa opcional) + `python scripts/validate_test_commands.py <contracts_dir> <repo_root>` (corre el test_command real de cada contrato y falla si algun exit code no es 0, Nivel 1 obligatorio) + `python scripts/scan_secrets.py <dir>` (escaneo determinista de credenciales filtradas por prefijo de proveedor conocido, capa opcional) + el `test_command` del contrato, local y en CI (matriz dual-OS, suite 2x); nivel 2 (opcional) = gate CCDD vía MCP `ccdd-complexity` (`lint_task_contract`, `run_integration_gate`) sobre el export de `scripts/export_gate_contract.py`. Ningún contrato se considera terminado hasta que pase el nivel 1.
5. **Precedencia del Budget**: ver [knowledge/validacion.md](../knowledge/validacion.md) — con gate manda su config firmada (el `budget` del frontmatter solo puede ser <=); sin gate, el `budget` es declarativo y el validador solo verifica su presencia.
6. **Ciclo de Vida del Contrato**: `draft` -> `validated` -> `implemented` -> `verified`; detalle y evidencia requerida en [knowledge/validacion.md](../knowledge/validacion.md).
7. **Contexto presupuestado (CCDD Nivel 2)**: Antes de implementar una tarea delegada, ensambla su contexto con `python scripts/assemble_context.py ccdd/context.json "<tarea>"` (añade `-v` para el contexto completo). El reporte de slots/guardrails que imprime forma parte de la evidencia y se pega en `.agents/logs/<task>-REPORT.md`. Un guardrail `on_fail: abort` (exit 2) bloquea la tarea: no continúes hasta resolverlo. La doc del ensamblador vive en el script; aquí solo se referencia por ruta.

Este archivo es la fuente única de verdad para cualquier agente, sea cual sea la herramienta que lo hospeda. `.cursorrules`, `.github/copilot-instructions.md`, `.clinerules` y `.windsurfrules` en la raíz del repo son punteros delgados a este mismo archivo (convención de cada herramienta), no una copia — si hay divergencia, este archivo manda. Para un humano que revisa lo que produjo un agente, ver [knowledge/supervision-humana.md](../knowledge/supervision-humana.md).

## Herramientas de diagnóstico opt-in (NO son gates)

Nivel 2 tambien dispone de [integracion nativa](../knowledge/native-level2.md)
para funciones Python. Las menciones de MCP en el resumen anterior describen una
via disponible, no un requisito. Si el proyecto exige Nivel 2, su ausencia/error
bloquea: no sustituirlo silenciosamente por Nivel 1. El perfil nativo identifica
su politica por commit; no autentica firmas de umbrales.

Tres herramientas de diagnóstico local, opt-in, que **no son gates y no corren en CI**: Nivel 1 sigue siendo **19 gates** y el conteo no cambia. Documentación a fondo en [knowledge/validacion.md](../knowledge/validacion.md) (secciones "Preflight", "Auditor de seals débiles" y "Recetas de arreglo por rule-id").

- `python scripts/preflight.py [--repo-root DIR] [--contract NAME]` — dry-run de los 20 gates (19 de Nivel 1 + `validate_attestation` local-only); una línea `PASS`/`FAIL`/`TIMEOUT` por gate + resumen `N/20`. Úsalo **antes de delegar o empezar trabajo**, para no entregarle a un agente un repo que ya rompe un gate. Modo `--contract`: 3 chequeos de un task contract (frontmatter, sello, `test_command`).
- `python scripts/audit_seals.py [contracts_dir] [--repo-root DIR] [--strict]` — auditor ADVISORY de "seals débiles": detecta oráculos congelados que el sello (`tests_sha256`) certifica como íntegros pero que no pueden fallar (6 reglas `WEAK_*`). Ranked source regions for a plain-language description, with source and file:line inline, budgeted to drop straight into context. This is the first move for almost every locate task.

By default query returns: ranked candidate fix sites (top hits as full function bodies), RELATED SITES, the COVERING TEST plus other tests over the same code (ALSO COVERING), SAME-CONCEPT LITERAL (every place the concept is named, tagged EDIT/CONSUMER/DOC), a VERIFY line (the narrowest test command for the file), and a CLOSED-SET WARNING when a switch over a sealed set would fail at runtime. The three reference blocks (container map, signature types, declaration card) are OFF by default because they cost turns in agent sessions; --reference-blocks all turns them on for interactive reading.

--verify-block off (or --omit-verify, or ENTIRE_GRAPH_VERIFY_BLOCK=off) removes the VERIFY block and nothing else: the test command and the run-once/fix/stop advice that rides with it. That advice would help an agent with no tool just as much, so it exists for fair A/B comparisons (both arms get it, or neither). JSON then omits verify_command and reports stats.verify_omitted. In agent format the freed bytes go to ranked results under the same --max-context-bytes, so off is a different selection, not the on payload with lines deleted.

--top-k caps normal results, including automatic related sites and covering tests, without changing retrieval strategy. Explicit --callee-hop may add called-helper results beyond that cap, under its existing byte-budget and ranked-source protections. --deep additionally runs the exhaustive sparse (BM25) pass and fuses it with the semantic ranking (slower, reads every eligible file).

Ranking returns one region per unit, which is right for code and wrong for whole prose documents: one markdown document can hold the answer across several distant regions. So for prose the unit is the SECTION, not the file — a document's headed sections are ranked against every other section on their own scores, exactly as independent files would be (--document-resolution ranks a document as one unit instead). Separately, and on prose of any shape including headed documents, when fewer distinct units match than --top-k asked for, the spare slots are spent returning finer regions of the same document as results of their own (multi-resolution retrieval) — strictly additive, so it never displaces a unit and never breaches --max-context-bytes. --single-resolution turns that off. The two stack: a headed document can be ranked by section AND have spare slots filled with promoted passages, so a prose payload may carry both.

# Reglas para Agentes de IA

Si eres un agente de IA interactuando con este repositorio, debes acatar las siguientes reglas:

1. **Metodología KDD Obligatoria**: Este repositorio utiliza Knowledge-Driven Development. Antes de escribir código, debes leer los contratos en `knowledge/contracts/` y la spec normativa de los nodos OKF en `knowledge/OKF-SPEC.md`.
2. **Carga la Skill Local**: Tienes disponible la skill `kdd-okf-ccdd-hybrid` en el directorio `.agents/skills/`. Debes adoptarla en tu contexto para entender cómo generar y validar los contratos híbridos OKF-CCDD.
3. **No dupliques contexto**: Utiliza enlaces de markdown relativos a `knowledge/` cuando necesites explicar el porqué de una implementación.
4. **Validación Determinista (dos niveles)**: la referencia canónica completa (niveles, gate multi-lenguaje, export, `tc-tests-frozen`) está en [knowledge/validacion.md](../knowledge/validacion.md) — léela antes de validar; esta regla no la duplica. Ningún contrato se considera terminado hasta que pase el nivel 1.
5. **Precedencia del Budget**: ver [knowledge/validacion.md](../knowledge/validacion.md) — con gate manda su config firmada (el `budget` del frontmatter solo puede ser <=); sin gate, el `budget` es declarativo y el validador solo verifica su presencia.
6. **Ciclo de Vida del Contrato**: `draft` -> `validated` -> `implemented` -> `verified`; detalle y evidencia requerida en [knowledge/validacion.md](../knowledge/validacion.md).

El reporte de slots/guardrails que imprime forma parte de la evidencia y se pega en `.agents/logs/<task>-REPORT.md`. Un guardrail `on_fail: abort` (exit 2) bloquea la tarea: no continúes hasta resolverlo. La doc del ensamblador vive en el script; aquí solo se referencia por ruta.

Este archivo es la fuente única de verdad para cualquier agente, sea cual sea la herramienta que lo hospeda. `.cursorrules`, `.github/copilot-instructions.md`, `.clinerules` y `.windsurfrules` en la raíz del repo son punteros delgados a este mismo archivo (convención de cada herramienta), no una copia — si hay divergencia, este archivo manda. By default query returns: ranked candidate fix sites (top hits as full function bodies), RELATED SITES, the COVERING TEST plus other tests over the same code (ALSO COVERING), SAME-CONCEPT LITERAL (every place the concept is named, tagged EDIT/CONSUMER/DOC), a VERIFY line (the narrowest test command for the file), and a CLOSED-SET WARNING when a switch over a sealed set would fail at runtime. The three reference blocks (container map, signature types, declaration card) are OFF by default because they cost turns in agent sessions; --reference-blocks all turns them on for interactive reading.

--verify-block off (or --omit-verify, or ENTIRE_GRAPH_VERIFY_BLOCK=off) removes the VERIFY block and nothing else: the test command and the run-once/fix/stop advice that rides with it. That advice would help an agent with no tool just as much, so it exists for fair A/B comparisons (both arms get it, or neither). JSON then omits verify_command and reports stats.verify_omitted. In agent format the freed bytes go to ranked results under the same --max-context-bytes, so off is a different selection, not the on payload with lines deleted.

--top-k caps normal results, including automatic related sites and covering tests, without changing retrieval strategy. Explicit --callee-hop may add called-helper results beyond that cap, under its existing byte-budget and ranked-source protections. --deep additionally runs the exhaustive sparse (BM25) pass and fuses it with the semantic ranking (slower, reads every eligible file).

Ranking returns one region per unit, which is right for code and wrong for whole prose documents: one markdown document can hold the answer across several distant regions. So for prose the unit is the SECTION, not the file — a document's headed sections are ranked against every other section on their own scores, exactly as independent files would be (--document-resolution ranks a document as one unit instead). Separately, and on prose of any shape including headed documents, when fewer distinct units match than --top-k asked for, the spare slots are spent returning finer regions of the same document as results of their own (multi-resolution retrieval) — strictly additive, so it never displaces a unit and never breaches --max-context-bytes. --single-resolution turns that off. The two stack: a headed document can be ranked by section AND have spare slots filled with promoted passages, so a prose payload may carry both.

Flags:
  --query <text>            The task or bug in one plain sentence; alternatively supply one final argument
  --repo <path>             Repository to search (default: current repo)
  --top-k <n>               Maximum normal results, including related/covering entries (--callee-hop may add helpers) (default: 10)
  --format text|json|ndjson|agent
                            Output format; text is tiered for reading, agent is compact (default: json)
  --head                    Search the committed tree (cached) instead of the working tree
  --profile syntax-only|fast|full
                            Parsing depth; use full for bug-fix/locate (call-graph active) (default: fast)
  --deep                    Also run the exhaustive BM25 pass and fuse it (slower)
  --callee-hop              Add called-helper results beyond --top-k, subject to byte-budget and ranked-source protections
  --single-resolution       One result per ranked unit; do not spend spare slots on finer regions of a prose document
  --document-resolution     Rank a prose document as one unit; do not rank its sections separately
  --max-context-bytes <n>   Output byte budget; 0 = unbounded. Unset with --format agent: the smallest of 4096/8192/16384 that shows the top hit whole, else 24576 (default: 24576)
  --reference-blocks all|container-map,signature-types,type-card
                            Turn reference blocks back on (off by default)
  --verify-block on|off     off removes the VERIFY block (suggested test command plus its run/fix/stop advice) in every format; exists for fair A/B comparisons against an arm with no tool. Env: ENTIRE_GRAPH_VERIFY_BLOCK (default: on)
  --omit-verify             Shorthand for --verify-block off
  --max-indexed-files <n>   Bound cold-search parsing to N files
  --index-all-files         Widen cold-search parsing to every file
  --cache-dir <path>        Override the committed-tree cache directory
  --no-cache                Disable the committed-tree cache

# Contract: assemble-context

## Intent
Portar el ensamblador de contexto CCDD Nivel 2 (probado en el proyecto origen, ver
[metodología de ejecución](../metodologia-ejecucion.md)) a esta plantilla: dado un contrato
JSON de slots y una tarea, produce contexto presupuestado, firmado y auditado desde la KB
OKF de `knowledge/`.

## Interface
```python
def assemble(contract: dict, task: str, base_dir: str) -> dict:
    """Ensambla el contexto. Devuelve dict con: slots (lista de reportes por slot:
    id, priority, status included|omitted, tokens, compaction, sign, selected),
    context (str), used, available, guardrails {ok, findings}.
    Lanza ValueError con mensaje claro ante contrato inválido; los guardrails
    on_fail=abort se reportan vía excepción dedicada o clave de error (documentar)."""
```
CLI: `python scripts/assemble_context.py <contract.json> "<tarea>" [-v]` — reporte por
slot + totales + guardrails; con `-v` además el contexto completo. Exit 0 ok · 2 contrato
inválido o guardrail abort · 1 I/O.

## Invariants
- Determinismo estricto: mismas entradas → stdout byte a byte idéntico (sin relojes, sin
  orden de dict no determinista; heurística 1 token ≈ 4 chars, documentada).
- Slots por prioridad ascendente; presupuesto global = max_tokens - output_reserve; topes
  max_tokens/min_tokens por slot; compaction `none`|`truncate`|`summarize`. **`truncate` y
  `summarize` son AMBOS corte por caracteres determinista (sin LLM, sin resumen semántico):
  solo difieren el marcador que dejan al cortar (`[...truncated]` vs `[...summarized]`).
  `summarize` se mantiene aceptado por compatibilidad con la plantilla publicada, pero el
  nombre es histórico, no descriptivo: no resume, corta igual que `truncate`.
- `sign: true` → sha256 del contenido compactado, primeros 12 hex.
- Providers dinámicos:
  - `okf_index`: knowledge/index.md.
  - `okf_nodes`: nodos con ranking determinista: score = 2 puntos por mención literal del
    nombre de archivo (sin .md) + 1 punto por cada tag del frontmatter que matchea como
    palabra en la tarea. Ordenados score desc, empate alfabético. Sin matches → fallback
    (todos, score 0, alfabético). Corte por nodo (no por concatenación): nodos enteros se
    incluyen mientras quepan; el primero que no cabe se compacta según modo del slot
    (`truncate`/`summarize`, con marcador); los siguientes se omiten.
  - Reporte honesto: slot `okf_nodes` declara `selected` = TODOS los nodos recuperados por
    el retriever, `sorted()` alfabético (compat: como el reporte previo, redundante a
    propósito — es el universo recuperado), y además `cut` (el nodo compactado, si lo hubo)
    y `omitted_nodes` (lista de omitidos, si los hubo) como subconjuntos declarados aparte;
    claves ausentes cuando no aplica. Partición: selected = incluidos enteros ∪ {cut} ∪
    omitted_nodes.
  - `budget.chars_per_token` opcional (entero ≥1, default 4): multiplica el costo en tokens;
    compartido entre `_tokens` y `_compact` desde UN solo lugar. Inválido → `ValueError`.
- Guardrails: `regex_deny` (cada patrón se evalúa con `re.search` de stdlib sobre el
  contexto ensamblado — es un patrón regex de verdad, no un substring literal; un patrón que
  no compila → `ValueError` que nombra el patrón, sin silencio ni fallback a literal;
  on_fail abort → exit 2) y `reference_check` (ruta `knowledge/...md` citada en la tarea que
  no existe → hallazgo). El reporte lista SOLO los guardrails configurados en el
  contrato/config: sin `regex_deny` configurado, la palabra `regex_deny` no aparece en el
  reporte.
- Solo stdlib; sin red; sin subprocess; sin escribir archivos (salida por stdout).

## Examples
- `python scripts/assemble_context.py ccdd/context.json "documentar la tabla users"` ->
  exit 0, reporte con `okf_nodes` incluyendo `users_table` (match por tag/mención).
- `assemble(contract, "tarea que cita knowledge/no-existe.md", ".")` -> guardrails con
  hallazgo de `reference_check` (nodo inexistente).
- `assemble(contract, "log: secret : value", ".")` con `regex_deny.patterns=["secret\\s*:"]`
  -> abort: el patrón regex matchea `secret :` (con espacio), que un substring literal
  `secret\s*:` no atraparía. Con `patterns=["["]` -> `ValueError` que nombra el patrón.
- `assemble(contract_sin_guardrails, "tarea", ".")` -> el reporte no menciona `regex_deny`
  ni `reference_check` (no configurados); `guardrails: ok` sin sub-líneas.
- Dos invocaciones idénticas del CLI -> stdout byte a byte idéntico.
- **Ranking (C15)**: task "explicar architecture_overview" → `okf_nodes` selecciona antes nodos
  cuyo nombre matchea (score 2) que nodos que matchean solo por tags (score 1). Empate →
  alfabético.
- **Per-node cutting (C15)**: presupuesto justo (p.ej. 900 tokens, 3 nodos de 500 cada uno)
  → primero entra nodo score 2 (entero), segundo aparece en `cut` (compactado), tercero en
  `omitted_nodes`. Sin presupuesto exigente → `cut` y `omitted_nodes` ausentes.
- **chars_per_token (C15)**: `budget.chars_per_token=REDACTED cuesta el doble → menos nodos caben.
  Default 4 (1 token ≈ 4 chars). Inválido (p.ej. 0, -1) → `ValueError` que nombra la clave.

## Do / Don't
- DO: portar la semántica del patrón probado (prioridad/presupuesto/compaction/firma).
- DO: mensajes de error con la causa exacta (qué clave falta, qué slot excede, qué patrón
  regex no compila).
- DO: que el reporte sea honesto — listar solo los guardrails configurados y declarar que
  `truncate`/`summarize` son corte por caracteres (no sobre-prometer con el nombre).
- DON'T: dependencias fuera de stdlib, red, subprocess, timestamps en la salida.
- DON'T: usar `pat in context` (substring literal) para `regex_deny`; usar `re.search`.
- DON'T: imprimir `regex_deny: ok`/`reference_check: ok` cuando ese guardrail no está
  configurado en el contrato.
- DON'T: modificar `scripts/validate_contracts.py`, `src/`, tests existentes o nodos OKF existentes.

## Tests
(Los tests están en `tests/test_assemble_context.py`: presupuesto respetado, prioridades,
truncado, min_tokens, firma estable, determinismo 2×, retriever por mención/tags/fallback,
regex_deny aborta, reference_check detecta y pasa, exit codes del CLI. Además (CTX-HONESTO,
T8): `regex_deny` evalúa con `re.search` — un patrón regex real como `secret\s*:` matchea
contenido que el substring literal no matchearía; un patrón que no compila lanza `ValueError`
que lo nombra; un patrón alfanumérico simple (sin metacaracteres regex) da el mismo veredicto
que antes; y el reporte omite los guardrails no configurados — sin `regex_deny` configurado
la palabra `regex_deny` no aparece.)

## Constraints
- PARAR y reportar si... el contrato JSON exigiera capacidades imposibles con stdlib puro,
  si hiciera falta red o subprocess para cumplir un criterio, o si un test existente del
  repo se rompiera con el cambio.

# OKF-SPEC — Open Knowledge Format (especificación de referencia)

OKF modela el conocimiento como **nodos**: archivos Markdown bajo `knowledge/`, interconectados por enlaces relativos. Esta es la spec normativa mínima para la plantilla KDD.

## 1. Nodo OKF

Un **nodo** es un archivo `.md` ubicado bajo `knowledge/` cuyo bloque inicial es **frontmatter YAML válido** delimitado por dos líneas `---`.

Reglas:
- El frontmatter **debe** estar presente y ser parseable como YAML.
- Tras el frontmatter sigue el cuerpo Markdown del nodo.
- Un nodo **debe** poder enlazarse desde `knowledge/index.md` (ver §5).

## 2. Frontmatter mínimo obligatorio

Todo nodo debe incluir estas claves, sin excepción:

| Clave         | Tipo     | Obligatoria | Descripción                                           |
|---------------|----------|-------------|-------------------------------------------------------|
| `type`        | string   | sí          | Uno de los tipos reconocidos (ver §3).                |
| `title`       | string   | sí          | Título humano del nodo.                               |
| `description` | string   | sí          | Resumen de una línea del contenido del nodo.          |
| `tags`        | string[] | sí          | Lista no vacía de etiquetas en minúsculas.            |

Claves adicionales (p. ej. `task`, `target`, `signature` en los contratos) son **permitidas** y específicas de cada tipo; esta spec no las restringe.

## 3. Tipos de nodo reconocidos

`type` debe ser exactamente uno de:

- `'Task Contract'` — contrato determinista para un agente efímero (CCDD). Vive típicamente bajo `knowledge/contracts/`.
- `'Data Model'` — modelo de datos (tablas, esquemas, entidades). Vive bajo `knowledge/data_models/`.
- `'Architecture'` — componente o vista de arquitectura del sistema. Vive bajo `knowledge/architecture/`.
- `'Concept'` — definición conceptual o especificación de referencia (esta spec lo es).
- `'Task'` — seguimiento operativo versionado en Git, separado del contrato aprobado; formato en [Tarea Git](data_models/git-task.md).

Cualquier otro valor de `type` se considera **inválido** para la plantilla.

## 4. Reglas de enlazado

- Los enlaces entre nodos son **enlaces Markdown relativos** (p. ej. `[texto](./architecture/overview.md)`).
- **Prohibido duplicar contenido de otro nodo.** Si la información ya vive en otro nodo, se **enlaza** al nodo fuente en lugar de reproducirla.
- Un enlace debe apuntar, dentro de `knowledge/`, a un archivo `.md` existente o a una carpeta existente. Un archivo existente con otra extensión (p. ej. `.txt`) es un enlace inválido. No se enlazan rutas externas al bundle como si fueran nodos.

## 5. Regla de indexado

- Todo nodo nuevo **debe** enlazarse desde `knowledge/index.md` (sección correspondiente a su carpeta/tipo).
- `index.md` es el catálogo de entrada al bundle; un nodo no enlazado desde `index.md` se considera huérfano.

## 6. Conformidad

Un nodo es **OKF-válido** si cumple simultáneamente: §1 (formato nodo), §2 (frontmatter mínimo), §3 (`type` reconocido), §4 (enlaces relativos, sin duplicación) y §5 (enlazado desde `index.md`).

# Validación de contratos — nodo canónico

Única fuente de verdad sobre cómo se valida un task contract en esta plantilla. El README, [.agents/AGENTS.md](../.agents/AGENTS.md) y la skill `kdd-okf-ccdd-hybrid` enlazan aquí en lugar de duplicar este contenido (regla §4 de [OKF-SPEC](./OKF-SPEC.md)).

## Nivel 1 — Incluido y obligatorio (local + CI)

La [extension de tiempo total del CI](ci-runtime.md) conserva los19 gates,
Ubuntu/Windows y las dos pasadas completas. Sustituye el mecanismo serial
de suite por un runner auditable por IDs, con procesos acotados solo bajo
opt-in y default serial para consumidores. Sus contratos y oraculos deben
tener baseline revisado antes de activar ese mecanismo.

La [ejecucion confiable](ci-audit-remediation.md) extrae el runtime revisado
fuera del checkout y conserva reportes nuevos por pasada. La publicacion de
[Pages](pages-ci-inventory.md) consume sus inventarios y los compara con un
discovery estricto del mismo SHA. Es una comprobacion de publicacion;
el catalogo de Nivel 1 sigue teniendo 19 gates.
