Former GitHub CEO Thomas Dohmke’s startup just unveiled a GitHub alternative
Date: Mon Oct 26 17:00:00 2026 UTC

Entire, a startup launched by former GitHub CEO Thomas Dohmke, has officially unveiled an alternative to the popular development platform. 
The new Git forge is designed specifically with agent-human collaboration in mind, according to the startup, and will offer users the same basic abilities as GitHub - albeit with a twist for the AI era.
Entire claims its platform is built on "fundamentally new primitives" compared to GitHub and other platforms. The system is built on a new distributed source control server compatible with Git, meaning that every developer has their own dedicated server. 
Using this method, the startup claims it pushes up to 89 times faster than GitHub and six times faster than Cursor's Origin. 
"This makes Entire the fastest Git forge in product today," the startup said in an announcement. "Developers can create, migrate, and natively host private repositories in the region of their choice, including the US, EU, India, and Australia."
Other basic functions like code reviews have received a sprucing up with the 'Trails' feature, according to Entire. While other platforms rely on a classic pull request model to review code changes, Entire will provide users with a "heads-up display similar to an airline pilot". 
This will include rolling, customized evals that are assessed and scored by agents with each code push, the company added. 
Notably, Entire also leverages continuous memory, which it said represents a "new approach" that allows agents and developer teams to sync sessions and prompts within the repository. 
The advantage here, according to Entire, is that data is constantly available and searchable for coding agents. This approach relies on two core components: a codebase graph that allows agents to "find answers faster" and reduce token consumption, and an "agentic brain". 
This essentially stores previous agent sessions and prompts within a system of memory that can be referred to or queried further down the line. 

Entire targets agentic orchestration gains

Dohmke said these features come in direct response to the growing use of agents in software development processes. 
JetBrains' Developer Ecosystem Survey found around 90% of developers now use AI coding agents at work on a weekly basis. More than two-thirds (68%), meanwhile, are using them on a daily basis. 
"The Pull Request revolutionized first open source and later enterprise software development. Instead of sending diffs and patches on email lists, developers could fork a repo and send their code changes back to the maintainer," he commented. 
"But agents now write almost all of it, faster and more complex than ever before."
Dohmke added that Entire treats the "idea, the agent trace, and the outcome of a developer's sessions as first-class artifacts for review alongside the code". 
The platform also uses multiple agents to conduct evals to ensure developers can confidently merge code without repeated reviews. 
"This allows coding agents to address findings in a loop, while the human developer validates the progress," he explained. "When all evals are satisfied, they can merge the code without needing to look at the code itself."

Dohmke's first move post-GitHub

The announcement marks the first big move by Entire since it launched earlier this year with an eye on building the "world's next developer platform for the era of AI". 
Entire hit the ground running in February backed by a $60 million seed round at a $300 million valuation. The investment round was led by Felic, with participation from Madrona, M12, 20VC, and Cherry Ventures. 
That announcement also marked Dohmke's first venture since departing GitHub as CEO. 
When he announced his departure in August 2025, Dohmke specifically noted that his "startup roots have begun tugging on me", prompting speculation about a new venture. 

A viable GitHub alternative?

While Entire frames itself as a viable alternative to GitHub, it faces stiff competition on this front, and not only from the aforementioned platform. 
As ITPro reported in August, vibe coding startup Cursor launched its own alternative to tap into what has become a highly lucrative market. 
When Cursor launched Origin, the company said it was "starting with the essentials", offering users much of the same basic features found in GitHub. Long-term, the plan is to provide "agent-native features". 
Alongside the launch, Entire revealed it has secured partnerships with Buildkite and Depot to ensure build and test pipelines "keep up with how fast agents ship". 
Entire said this will allow users to move off GitHub Actions by converting existing workflows using Buildkite's bk pipeline or Depot CI, enabling them to subscribe the repository in its own platform. 
This move by Entire mirrors Cursor, which also announced partnerships with Depot and Buildkite to build a broader "app ecosystem" aimed at tempting users away from GitHub.

## Workflow triggers

Workflow triggers are events that cause a workflow to run. These events can be:

  * Events that occur in your workflow's repository
  * Events that occur outside of GitHub and trigger a `repository_dispatch` event on GitHub
  * Scheduled times
  * Manual

For example, you can configure your workflow to run when a push is made to the default branch of your repository, when a release is created, or when an issue is opened.

Workflow triggers are defined with the `on` key. For more information, see Workflow syntax for GitHub Actions.

The following steps occur to trigger a workflow run:

  1. An event occurs on your repository. The event has an associated commit SHA and Git ref.
  2. GitHub searches the `.github/workflows` directory in the root of your repository for workflow files that are present in the associated commit SHA or Git ref of the event.
  3. A workflow run is triggered for any workflows that have `on:` values that match the triggering event. Some events also require the workflow file to be present on the default branch of the repository in order to run.

Each workflow run will use the version of the workflow that is present in the associated commit SHA or Git ref of the event. Sí, **podemos usar GitHub Actions**. Mi respuesta anterior fue demasiado restrictiva.

Hay dos opciones:

- **Repositorio de laboratorio en GitHub, reflejado en Entire:** Actions ejecuta las pruebas y Entire puede exigir sus resultados mediante el gate **Checks**, disponible para mirrors de GitHub. Es la opción con integración documentada. [Documentación](https://docs.entire.com/guides/ci/checks)
- **Mantener el repositorio nativo de Entire:** Actions puede actuar como ejecutor externo, descargando la revisión exacta. Pero necesitaríamos conectar sus resultados con el observador; las integraciones directas documentadas para repositorios nativos son Buildkite y Depot. [Integraciones](https://docs.entire.com/guides/ci/overview)

Para nuestro caso, recomiendo añadir un laboratorio privado en GitHub y reflejarlo en Entire, conservando el laboratorio nativo para probar sus controles específicos. Los repositorios originales seguirían intactos.

Esto permitiría avanzar con CI; seguirían pendientes la segunda identidad y los adaptadores restantes.

# Laboratorio de KDD Entire

Este directorio es un laboratorio separado de D:/Repo/kdd_2 y D:/Repo/kdd-entire.
No ejecutar escrituras, hooks, agentes ni configuración en esos repositorios.

Leer README.md y config/scenario-readiness.json antes de ejecutar. No cambiar
el catálogo congelado, los expected ni el lock para conseguir resultados verdes.
La copia candidata es candidate/; trusted/, config/ y evidence/ son del operador.
No ejecutar código del candidato desde el proceso observador ni darle credenciales.

Las operaciones remotas autorizadas se limitan al proyecto kdd-entire-lab-c7f091.
Consultar entire agent-help y la ayuda del comando. Mantener la descripción del
Trail vigente; publicar hallazgos de revisión como findings, no como comentarios.

El usuario confirmó que no dispone de CI ni otra cuenta. No crear identidades
ficticias, activar proveedores de pago ni presentar sesiones del mismo principal
como aprobación independiente. Este laboratorio NO está listo para los 48 casos.

Un PASS solo corresponde a evidencia de la operación realmente ejecutada.
Errores de autenticación, transporte, timeout y adaptadores ausentes no son
rechazos de seguridad. Las autopruebas con mocks no son escenarios reales.

El observador tiene independencia de código/proceso, pero utiliza la misma cuenta
del operador: no es una segunda autoridad ni un sandbox frente a un administrador.
Cambiar esa frontera exige otra identidad/ejecutor, no un ajuste de etiquetas.
# Laboratorio aislado de kdd-entire

Configuración real del 2026-10-28. La batería completa todavía no es ejecutable:
**3 escenarios reales PASS, 45 NOT_RUN, 0 FAIL; complete=false, exit 2**.
Los 8 controles positivos del catálogo siguen pendientes. Esto no certifica KDD
ni representa una batería de 48 escenarios aprobada.

El usuario confirmó que no tiene CI ni una segunda cuenta. Además faltan los
adaptadores del flujo de aceptación, alcance, sesiones, consumo y cierre verificado.
El detalle de cada uno de los 48 casos está en
[scenario-readiness.json](config/scenario-readiness.json). Contiene el procedimiento
original, sus capacidades ausentes y las razones de bloqueo.

Los repositorios de trabajo permanecen fuera del laboratorio. Se exportó con
`git archive` la revisión `29bb09cedbaff923eaa32b61e2ced77a5ae91808` de
`D:/Repo/kdd-entire`, sin copiar su .git, hooks ni configuración de remotes.
No se modificó D:/Repo/kdd_2 ni D:/Repo/kdd-entire.

| Componente | Configuración aplicada |
|---|---|
| Proyecto privado separado | kdd-entire-lab-c7f091 |

| CI / agentes de pago | sin conexión / sin activar |

`candidate/` contiene el checkout atacable. `trusted/` contiene una copia congelada
del catálogo y del ejecutor, el actuador y el observador. `config/trust-lock.json`
fija sus hashes y los de los recibos de las acciones; no contiene secretos.
`evidence/` conserva las consultas, acciones y resultados reales.

> ## Documentation Index

# Install the Entire GitHub App

> Authorize the Entire GitHub App and choose which repositories Entire can access.

Entire uses the GitHub App to access the repositories you choose.

## When You Need This

Configure GitHub App access when you want to:

* make a GitHub repository appear in Entire
* create a repository mirror
* let Entire read repository and checkpoint activity
* let Entire verify GitHub collaborator access for mirror permissions

GitHub App access controls which GitHub repositories Entire can see. It does not move, delete, or replace the GitHub repository.

## Configure GitHub App Access

Choose the flow that matches where the repository lives.

**Personal Repository**

Use this when the repository is owned by your GitHub account.

In entire.com, open repository setup and choose **Configure GitHub App**.

GitHub opens the Entire GitHub App settings. From there, choose either:

* **All repositories**, if Entire should be able to access every repository in your account
* **Only select repositories**, if Entire should only access specific repositories

Save the GitHub App configuration, then return to entire.com.

**Organization Repository**

Use this when the repository is owned by a GitHub organization.

For organization repositories, a GitHub organization admin must install or update the Entire GitHub App.

In entire.com, open repository setup and choose **Configure GitHub App**.

GitHub opens the Entire GitHub App settings. From there, the organization admin can choose either:

* **All repositories**, if Entire should be able to access every repository in the organization
* **Only select repositories**, if Entire should only access specific repositories

Save the GitHub App configuration, then return to entire.com.

After the app is installed and allowed to access a repository, team members can use repositories they already have GitHub collaborator access to.

## What the Flow Looks Like

GitHub asks you to authorize Entire before you choose which repositories the app can access.

![GitHub authorization screen for Entire](https://mintcdn.com/entire/fgG56b7zcMZgFdOf/images/github-auth-light.png?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=fgG56b7zcMZgFdOf\&q=85\&s=2dfdf53f0c446e17e59d8bcb0d8f67a5)

After authorization, return to entire.com and select the repositories you want to connect.

![Repository selector in entire.com](https://mintcdn.com/entire/fgG56b7zcMZgFdOf/images/repo-selector-light.png?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=fgG56b7zcMZgFdOf\&q=85\&s=6d17f344c1f736e666d4214d438e19c9)

## Verify Access

For a repository to appear in Entire or be available for mirroring:

* the Entire GitHub App must be installed for the account or organization
* the app must be allowed to access that repository
* your GitHub account must have access to that repository

If the repository does not appear after configuring access, confirm that you are viewing the correct GitHub account or organization and that the repository is included in the GitHub App access list.

## Permissions

The Entire GitHub App requests these permissions:

**Repository permissions**

| Permission | Purpose |
| - | - |
| Administration: read | Read repository settings, teams, and collaborators. |
| Checks: read | Read check status for repository activity and review context. |
| Commit statuses: read | Read commit status information. |
| Contents: read/write | Read repository contents and support Git operations that require repository content access. |
| Pull requests: read/write | Read and support pull request workflows, comments, labels, assignees, and related metadata. |

**Organization permissions**

| Permission | Purpose |
| - | - |
| Members: read | Read organization members and teams. |

> [!NOTE]
>
> Checkpoint data is created locally by the Entire CLI and stored in your repository as Git refs under `refs/entire/checkpoints/`, or on the `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch in repositories that use the legacy branch backend. The GitHub App does not create local checkpoints for you.

## Mirrors

Repository mirrors require GitHub App access to the source GitHub repository.

After GitHub App access is configured, you can create a mirror from entire.com or the CLI:

```bash theme={null}
entire repo mirror add /gh/OWNER/REPO
```

GitHub App access controls which repositories Entire can see. User mirror access follows GitHub collaborator permissions and syncs hourly. See [Mirror Access and Permissions](https://docs.entire.com/guides/repositories/mirror-access-and-permissions.md).

## Remove Access

If you uninstall the Entire GitHub App or remove a repository from its access list:

* the repository may stop appearing in entire.com
* Entire cannot create or update mirrors for that repository
* Entire cannot sync new checkpoint activity from that repository
* existing checkpoint data already stored in Entire remains visible according to your current access settings
* local Git branches and local checkpoint data are not deleted

## Continue With

> **[Mirrors](https://docs.entire.com/guides/repositories/mirrors.md)**

# Mirror Repositories in entire.com

> Configure GitHub access, choose repositories, and create mirrors from entire.com.

Use entire.com when you want to configure GitHub access, mirror, and choose repositories from the web interface. This guide covers the web flow. For the command-line flow, see [Mirrors in CLI](https://docs.entire.com/guides/repositories/mirrors-in-cli.md).

## Before You Start

Make sure you have:

* a GitHub account connected to Entire
* access to the GitHub repository you want to mirror
* a GitHub organization admin available if the repository belongs to an organization and the Entire GitHub App has not been installed yet

## Configure GitHub Access

In entire.com, open the repository setup flow and choose **Configure GitHub App**.

GitHub opens the Entire GitHub App configuration. From there, an organization admin can install the app or update its repository access.

![Configure GitHub access in entire.com](https://mintcdn.com/entire/D9_zdkuUfghOz4a4/images/mirrors-entire-io-configure-github-access.png?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=D9_zdkuUfghOz4a4\&q=85\&s=f8bf6d3ee01e10f97f39e528a632776e)

Choose either:

* **All repositories**, if Entire should be able to access every repository in the account or organization
* **Only select repositories**, if Entire should only access specific repositories

Save the GitHub App configuration, then return to entire.com.

## Select Repositories

After GitHub access is configured, entire.com shows the repositories that are available to mirror.

Select the repositories you want to make available in Entire. If a repository does not appear, confirm that:

* the Entire GitHub App can access the repository
* your GitHub account has access to the repository
* you are viewing the correct account or organization

For more help, see [Troubleshooting](https://docs.entire.com/guides/repositories/troubleshooting.md).

## Choose Data Residency

Choose the region where Entire stores and serves the repository mirror. Entire currently supports mirroring in regions such as the United States, the European Union, the UK, India, Australia, and Brazil.

<video autoPlay loop muted playsInline poster="/images/videos/mirror-in-entire-com.jpg">
  <source src="https://mintcdn.com/entire/yKSEaBtqgPAkqkkW/images/videos/mirror-in-entire-com.mp4?fit=max&auto=format&n=yKSEaBtqgPAkqkkW&q=85&s=8902b9c1d2c3713a09500a8e0e6263b1" type="video/mp4" />
</video>

Adding regions to a connected GitHub repository and waiting for them to sync.

Use the region required by your team's security, compliance, or latency needs. You can choose a region per repository before continuing.

![Choose data residency for mirrored repositories in entire.com](https://mintcdn.com/entire/D9_zdkuUfghOz4a4/images/mirrors-entire-io-choose-data-residency.png?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=D9_zdkuUfghOz4a4\&q=85\&s=825dddcf87101da8f27be767ccbd8308)

## Continue to Entire

After you choose repositories and data residency, continue to the repositories tab in entire.com.

The mirrored repositories appear in the repository list. From there, your team can use entire.com to inspect repository activity and agents can use the mirror as a regional Git remote.

![Mirrored repositories listed in entire.com](https://mintcdn.com/entire/D9_zdkuUfghOz4a4/images/mirrors-entire-io-repositories-list.png?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=D9_zdkuUfghOz4a4\&q=85\&s=3472e5d789db4f9db88682fbf3b9fc0c)

## If You Are Not an Org Admin

If you are not a GitHub organization admin, you may not be able to add or remove repositories from the GitHub App configuration.

You can still continue to entire.com and use repositories that an admin has already made available. If the repository you need is missing, ask a GitHub organization admin to configure the Entire GitHub App for that repository.

![Non-admin repository access state in entire.com](https://mintcdn.com/entire/D9_zdkuUfghOz4a4/images/mirrors-entire-io-not-org-admin.png?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=D9_zdkuUfghOz4a4\&q=85\&s=b0802a9c600553876a4323422c620413)

For the full GitHub App permission model, see [GitHub App Access](https://docs.entire.com/guides/repositories/github-app-access.md). For GitHub-synced mirror access and hourly collaborator sync, see [Mirror Access and Permissions](https://docs.entire.com/guides/repositories/mirror-access-and-permissions.md).

# Install the Entire GitHub App

> Authorize the Entire GitHub App and choose which repositories Entire can access.

Entire uses the GitHub App to access the repositories you choose.

## When You Need This

Configure GitHub App access when you want to:

* make a GitHub repository appear in Entire
* create a repository mirror
* let Entire read repository and checkpoint activity
* let Entire verify GitHub collaborator access for mirror permissions

GitHub App access controls which GitHub repositories Entire can see. It does not move, delete, or replace the GitHub repository.

## Configure GitHub App Access

Choose the flow that matches where the repository lives.

**Personal Repository**

Use this when the repository is owned by your GitHub account.

In entire.com, open repository setup and choose **Configure GitHub App**.

GitHub opens the Entire GitHub App settings. From there, choose either:

* **All repositories**, if Entire should be able to access every repository in your account
* **Only select repositories**, if Entire should only access specific repositories

Save the GitHub App configuration, then return to entire.com.

**Organization Repository**

Use this when the repository is owned by a GitHub organization.

For organization repositories, a GitHub organization admin must install or update the Entire GitHub App.

In entire.com, open repository setup and choose **Configure GitHub App**.

GitHub opens the Entire GitHub App settings. From there, the organization admin can choose either:

* **All repositories**, if Entire should be able to access every repository in the organization
* **Only select repositories**, if Entire should only access specific repositories

Save the GitHub App configuration, then return to entire.com.

After the app is installed and allowed to access a repository, team members can use repositories they already have GitHub collaborator access to.

## What the Flow Looks Like

GitHub asks you to authorize Entire before you choose which repositories the app can access.

![GitHub authorization screen for Entire](https://mintcdn.com/entire/fgG56b7zcMZgFdOf/images/github-auth-light.png?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=fgG56b7zcMZgFdOf\&q=85\&s=2dfdf53f0c446e17e59d8bcb0d8f67a5)

After authorization, return to entire.com and select the repositories you want to connect.

![Repository selector in entire.com](https://mintcdn.com/entire/fgG56b7zcMZgFdOf/images/repo-selector-light.png?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=fgG56b7zcMZgFdOf\&q=85\&s=6d17f344c1f736e666d4214d438e19c9)

## Verify Access

For a repository to appear in Entire or be available for mirroring:

* the Entire GitHub App must be installed for the account or organization
* the app must be allowed to access that repository
* your GitHub account must have access to that repository

If the repository does not appear after configuring access, confirm that you are viewing the correct GitHub account or organization and that the repository is included in the GitHub App access list.

## Permissions

The Entire GitHub App requests these permissions:

**Repository permissions**

| Permission | Purpose |
| - | - |
| Administration: read | Read repository settings, teams, and collaborators. |
| Checks: read | Read check status for repository activity and review context. |
| Commit statuses: read | Read commit status information. |
| Contents: read/write | Read repository contents and support Git operations that require repository content access. |
| Pull requests: read/write | Read and support pull request workflows, comments, labels, assignees, and related metadata. |

**Organization permissions**

| Permission | Purpose |
| - | - |
| Members: read | Read organization members and teams. |

> [!NOTE]
>
> Checkpoint data is created locally by the Entire CLI and stored in your repository as Git refs under `refs/entire/checkpoints/`, or on the `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch in repositories that use the legacy branch backend. The GitHub App does not create local checkpoints for you.

## Mirrors

Repository mirrors require GitHub App access to the source GitHub repository.

After GitHub App access is configured, you can create a mirror from entire.com or the CLI:

```bash theme={null}
entire repo mirror add /gh/OWNER/REPO
```

GitHub App access controls which repositories Entire can see. User mirror access follows GitHub collaborator permissions and syncs hourly. See [Mirror Access and Permissions](https://docs.entire.com/guides/repositories/mirror-access-and-permissions.md).

## Remove Access

If you uninstall the Entire GitHub App or remove a repository from its access list:

* the repository may stop appearing in entire.com
* Entire cannot create or update mirrors for that repository
* Entire cannot sync new checkpoint activity from that repository
* existing checkpoint data already stored in Entire remains visible according to your current access settings
* local Git branches and local checkpoint data are not deleted

Scheduled events can be delayed during periods of high loads of GitHub Actions workflow runs.

High load times include the start of every hour. If the load is sufficiently high enough, some queued jobs may be dropped. To decrease the chance of delay, schedule your workflow to run at a different time of the hour. For more information, see Events that trigger workflows.

### Scheduled workflow stopped running

A scheduled (`cron`) workflow can stop running even though it is still enabled and manual or `workflow_dispatch` runs still work.

This can happen when the workflow's associated `actor` account is suspended, deleted, or deprovisioned. To restart it, a user with `write` access to the repository can commit a change to the `cron` schedule. See Events that trigger workflows.

### Filtering and diff limits

Specific events allow for filtering by branch, tag, and/or paths you can customize. Workflow run creation will be skipped if the filter conditions apply to filter out the workflow.

You can use special characters with filters. For more information, see Workflow syntax for GitHub Actions.

For path filtering, evaluating diffs is limited to the first 3,000 files. If there are files changed that are not matched in the first 3,000 files returned by the filter, the workflow will not be run. For more information, see Workflow syntax for GitHub Actions.

## Troubleshoot workflow execution

Workflow execution involves any issues seen after the workflow was triggered and a workflow run has been created.

### Debugging job conditions

If a job was skipped unexpectedly, or ran when you expected it to be skipped, you can view the expression evaluation to understand why:

  1. Click on the job in the workflow run.
  2. Download the log archive from the job's menu.
  3. Open the `JOB-NAME/system.txt` file.
  4. Look for the `Evaluating`, `Expanded`, and `Result` lines.

The `Expanded` line shows the actual runtime values that were substituted into your `if` condition, making it clear why the expression evaluated to `true` or `false`.

For more information, see Viewing job condition expression logs.

### Canceling Workflows

If standard cancellation through the UI or API does not process as expected, there may be a conditional statement configured for your running workflow job(s) that causes it to not cancel.

In these cases, you can leverage the API to force cancel the run. For more information, see REST API endpoints for workflow runs.

A common cause can be using the `always()` status check function which returns `true`, even on cancellation. An alternative is to use the inverse of the `cancelled()` function, `${{ !cancelled() }}`.

For more information, see Using conditions to control job execution and Canceling a workflow run.

If a run remains queued or in progress after cancellation attempts, it may be stuck in an abnormal state rather than continuing because of `always()`. Signs include no jobs being created, the UI displaying "Failed to cancel workflow", or the `cancel` or `force-cancel` REST API endpoints returning HTTP `500` or `409`.

Self-service cancellation, including force cancellation, may not clear a stuck or out-of-sync workflow run or check suite. If your repository uses concurrency, the stuck run can continue blocking later runs in the same concurrency group. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Workflow cancellation reference

Find information on the steps GitHub takes to cancel a workflow run.

When canceling a workflow run, you may be running other software that uses resources related to the workflow run. To help you free up resources related to the workflow run, it may help to understand the steps GitHub performs to cancel a workflow run.

  1. To cancel the workflow run, the server re-evaluates `if` conditions for all currently running jobs. If the condition evaluates to `true`, the job will not get canceled. For example, the condition `if: always()` would evaluate to true and the job continues to run. When there is no condition, that is the equivalent of the condition `if: success()`, which only runs if the previous step finished successfully.
  2. For jobs that need to be canceled, the server sends a cancellation message to all the runner machines with jobs that need to be canceled.
  3. For jobs that continue to run, the server re-evaluates `if` conditions for the unfinished steps. If the condition evaluates to `true`, the step continues to run. You can use the `cancelled` expression to apply a status check of `cancelled()`. For more information, see Evaluate expressions in workflows and actions.
  4. For steps that need to be canceled, the runner machine sends `SIGINT/Ctrl-C` to the step's entry process (`node` for JavaScript actions, `docker` for container actions, and `bash/cmd/pwd` when using `run` in a step). If the process doesn't exit within 7500 ms, the runner will send `SIGTERM/Ctrl-Break` to the process, then wait for 2500 ms for the process to exit. If the process is still running, the runner kills the process tree.
  5. After the 5 minute cancellation timeout period, the server will forcibly terminate all jobs and steps marked for cancellation that are still running.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

With no arguments, launches an interactive wizard: pick repos to mirror, pick one or more regions, then creates every (repo, region) mirror in parallel and prints the clone URLs. --cluster requires a <repo>.

With a <repo>, places it on every cluster named by --cluster — repeat the flag or comma-separate the hosts — in parallel, then waits for each to become usable. Pass --no-wait to return as soon as the placements are registered. Idempotent on (repo, cluster), so naming a cluster the repo is already on reports it rather than failing.

When --cluster is omitted, an interactive terminal offers the available clusters as a multi-select; non-interactive runs default to aws-us-east-2.entire.io.

With an /et/ ref, places replicas of an Entire-native repo and waits for each to be seeded. A native mirror goes in a region other than the repo's own, so only those clusters are offered and --cluster has no default there: non-interactive runs must name one.

Every cluster is attempted: one that fails does not stop the others, and the command exits non-zero naming the ones that did.

Repository references name their forge: /gh/<owner>/<repo> for a GitHub mirror, /et/<project>/<repo> for an Entire-native repository.

Usage:
  entire repo mirror add [repo] [flags]

Examples:
  entire repo mirror add
  entire repo mirror add /gh/octocat/hello-world
  entire repo mirror add /gh/octocat/hello-world --cluster aws-us-east-2.entire.io
  entire repo mirror add /gh/octocat/hello-world --cluster aws-us-east-2.entire.io,aws-eu-central-1.entire.io
  entire repo mirror add /et/acme/web --cluster aws-eu-central-1.entire.io

Flags:
      --cluster strings    Cluster host(s) to mirror onto; repeat or comma-separate for several (a terminal offers a multi-select when omitted; other runs use aws-us-east-2.entire.io)
  -h, --help               help for add
      --no-wait            Return once the placement is registered, without waiting for the initial clone
      --timeout duration   How long to wait for mirror request submission, placement, and clone readiness (0 waits indefinitely) (default 30m0s)

Queue a fresh sync of a GitHub mirror on every cluster it is placed on, so a mirror that has fallen behind its upstream catches up without waiting for the next GitHub event.

This is also the check after fixing a block. When GitHub refused the Entire app's access while syncing (an org IP allow list, or a suspension hit mid-sync — `entire repo view` shows which), the server probes GitHub first: if the block has been lifted it clears the block and queues the sync; if not, nothing is queued and the command reports what still needs fixing.

Requires write access to the GitHub repository. Serves /gh/ references only: an Entire-native repository has no upstream to sync from.

--json prints the server's response (mirrorId, status) plus the repo.

+# Laboratorio privado KDD: GitHub Actions + Entire
+
+Fecha: 2026-10-28. Repositorio nuevo y aislado; no modifica D:/Repo/kdd_2 ni
+D:/Repo/kdd-entire. El usuario pidió dejar los workflows preparados y pausados
+después de que GitHub bloqueara su ejecución por presupuesto de Actions.
+
+- GitHub: https://github.com/MauricioPerera/kdd-entire-lab-c7f091
+- Mirror privado: https://entire.com/gh/mauricioperera/kdd-entire-lab-c7f091
+- Trail: https://entire.com/gh/mauricioperera/-/trails/3
+- Change de comprobación: https://entire.com/gh/mauricioperera/-/trails/3/changes/kdd-entire-lab-c7f091/1
+- PR de laboratorio: https://github.com/MauricioPerera/kdd-entire-lab-c7f091/pull/1
+
+## Configuración aplicada
+
+El mirror está ready en aws-us-east-2. Se habilitaron Trails y el gate Checks,
+bloqueante, con nombre exacto requerido `kdd-deterministic`, todos los checks
+reportados deben pasar y bypass `nobody`. Este perfil aísla la CI: approvals,
+findings y up_to_date están deshabilitados exclusivamente en este mirror nuevo.
+No representa la política final de KDD y no modifica las políticas del laboratorio
+nativo anterior ni las de los repositorios originales.
+
+El plan actual devuelve HTTP 403 al consultar la protección de ramas privadas y
+pide GitHub Pro o un repositorio público. Se mantiene el repositorio privado;
+no se contrató un plan ni se cambiaron presupuestos. Por tanto, el administrador
+de GitHub conserva capacidad para cambiar workflows y ramas sin esa protección.
+
+## Workflows preparados
+
+`lab.yml` valida el instrumento en Ubuntu y Windows y publica el inventario de
+los 48 escenarios. Un inventario correcto no significa que esos escenarios hayan
+pasado. `fixtures.yml` ejecuta un comprobador determinista contra datos JSON de
+una revisión exacta y conserva el número efectivo de pruebas, errores y skips.
+
+Ambos workflows están **disabled_manually**, por pedido del usuario. No hay
+runners propios instalados ni credenciales de Entire o personales en Actions.
+Los tokens de jobs tienen `contents: read`; checkout no persiste credenciales.
+Las acciones están fijadas por SHA. El ejecutor de fixtures se descarga siempre
+del commit aprobado `4b6eec0b743c63663d954b7b9372b84107c20d09`; el candidato
+solo aporta `.lab/fixture.json`, que se lee como datos y nunca se ejecuta.
+
+El primer run fue rechazado antes de iniciar jobs:
+https://github.com/MauricioPerera/kdd-entire-lab-c7f091/actions/runs/40788301009
+
+GitHub informó: “The job was not started because an Actions budget is preventing
+further use.” No hubo runner, steps ni pruebas ejecutadas. Ese fallo de arranque
+no cuenta como una prueba funcional fallida ni como un ataque detectado.
+
+## Batería y preparación de casos
+
+El [catálogo](adversarial/catalog.json) conserva los 48 escenarios y sus expected
+originales. SHA-256: `8422abb09bf6a76163f41e5f36102f567efcd578855bf0c4028c5241085fa54b`.
+Hay 36 autopruebas locales sintéticas del instrumento aprobadas. Los 48 casos del
+perfil GitHub permanecen NOT_RUN; los 3 PASS del laboratorio nativo anterior son
+evidencia separada y no se atribuyen a este mirror ni a otra revisión.
+
+| Fixture preparada | Uso previsto, todavía no ejecutado |
+|---|---|
+| mode=pass, answer=4 | OK-08: prueba efectiva aprobada en la revisión actual |
+| mode=fail, answer=3 | CI-03: fallo determinista real |
+| mode=skip | CI-06: todas las pruebas omitidas aunque el proceso termine 0 |
+| mode=hold | CI-02/04/05: observar pendiente, cancelar o agotar timeout real |
+| mode=race | CI-09: cambiar head durante la ejecución |
+| check ausente / anterior | CI-01/07: conservar diferencia entre revisión actual y resultado viejo |
+
+Las fixtures no sustituyen los actuadores y observaciones de cada escenario.
+Faltan, entre otros, las pruebas con identidad independiente, protección de
+aceptación, sesiones/consumo y cierre verificado. CI-10 describe una excepción
+de plugins nativos: no debe certificarse simulándola con un mirror de GitHub.
+
+## Observación independiente
+
+`ci/observe_configuration.py` se despliega fuera del checkout, bajo
+`C:/Users/Administrador/.codex/labs/kdd-entire-github-20261028-c7f091/operator/`.
+Se fijan sus bytes por SHA-256 antes de cargarlo. Solo ejecuta GET sobre este
+repositorio, el mirror y los IDs concretos del laboratorio; no ejecuta código
+candidato ni copia expected para producir resultados. Conserva las capturas por
+hash fuera del checkout y contrasta los testigos Git de los repositorios originales.
+
+El observador tiene independencia de fuente/proceso; sigue usando la misma
+identidad del operador. No proporciona una segunda aprobación humana ni una
+frontera de seguridad frente al administrador de la máquina.
+
+Entire devuelve mergeable=false y Checks pending/not_run para la revisión sin
+checks. Las operaciones CLI show/merge devolvieron además 403 de acceso, aunque
+la lectura por repo ID y el resync del mirror funcionaron. No se confunde ese
+403 con un rechazo del gate ni se declara probada la integración end-to-end.
+
+## Reanudar cuando el usuario habilite presupuesto
+
+```powershell
+gh workflow enable lab.yml --repo MauricioPerera/kdd-entire-lab-c7f091
+gh workflow run lab.yml --repo MauricioPerera/kdd-entire-lab-c7f091 --ref main
+gh workflow enable fixtures.yml --repo MauricioPerera/kdd-entire-lab-c7f091
+gh workflow run fixtures.yml --repo MauricioPerera/kdd-entire-lab-c7f091 --ref main
+```
+
+Primero comprobar el control positivo y sus pruebas efectivas. Después ejecutar
+las variantes negativas en ramas de laboratorio, confirmar el SHA y el resultado
+con la API de GitHub y leer el gate de Entire. Los errores de transporte, permisos,
+presupuesto, runner ausente o timeout del observador conservan estado inconcluso.
+El sistema solo puede declarar la batería completa tras ejecutar y aprobar los
+48 procedimientos canónicos, incluidos sus 8 controles positivos.
*** End Patch"));

Make an authenticated HTTP request to an Entire API and print the JSON response.

These endpoints are internal and can change shape without notice; where a
purpose-built command exists, its output is the stable interface.

The CLI attaches the right bearer token and dials the right host for the
chosen backend, so you don't have to plumb auth yourself:

  --to core   the control plane (default): orgs, repos, mirrors, clusters, /me
  --to cell   your home entire-api cell: /me/* activity, repo aggregates

Use --jurisdiction <slug> (e.g. us, eu) to reach a specific jurisdiction's
entire-api cell instead of your home one; it implies --to cell.

Both backends act as ENTIRE_TOKEN when set, else the selected login
(--context, else $ENTIRE_CONTEXT, else the active context), so a staging
login reaches staging's control plane and cells. The cell host comes from
environment's cluster listing; an explicit ENTIRE_API_BASE_URL names the
data host directly instead.

<path> is the full path on that host, e.g. /api/v1/clusters. These
placeholders are filled from the current repo's origin remote:
  {owner} {repo}   the GitHub owner / repo
  {repo_id}        the repo's Entire ULID (from its mirror) — cells key on this

The method is GET unless a field/body is given (then POST); override with -X.

Usage:
  entire api <path> [flags]

Examples:
  entire api /api/v1/clusters
  entire api --to cell /api/v1/me/activity
  entire api --jurisdiction eu /api/v1/me/activity
  entire api --to cell "/api/v1/me/recap?repo={repo_id}"
  entire api -X POST /api/v1/projects -f name=demo

Flags:
  -F, --field stringArray       add a typed parameter in key=value format; true/false/null/numbers are converted (repeatable)
  -H, --header stringArray      add a request header in key:value format (repeatable)
  -h, --help                    help for api
  -i, --include                 print the response status line and headers too
      --input string            file with the request body ("-" for stdin)
  -j, --jurisdiction string     target a specific jurisdiction's cell (e.g. us, eu) instead of your home cell; implies --to cell
  -X, --method string           HTTP method (default GET, or POST when a field/body is given)
  -f, --raw-field stringArray   add a string parameter in key=value format (repeatable)
      --to string               which backend to call: core or cell (default "core")

Global Flags:
      --context name   Act as this saved login name for this command only — including the git and agent processes it spawns — instead of the active context (entire auth contexts lists them)

## Le Git Graph - Commits Graph for GitHub

A browser extension that displays the git graph for any GitHub repository.

## Demo

## Installation

Install the extension from the link -

For Google Chrome, Opera, Vivaldi, Brave, and Microsoft Edge:

https://chrome.google.com/webstore/detail/le-git-graph-commits-grap/joggkdfebigddmaagckekihhfncdobff

For Mozilla Firefox:

https://addons.mozilla.org/firefox/addon/le-git-graph-github-git-graph/

After installation, open any GitHub repository and a new 'Commits' tab will be visible.

Open the commits tab and follow the prompt to authenticate with your GitHub account.

## Why does it need write access

The extension asks for permission in the level `repo - read and write`

Le Git Graph requires only read access to public or private repositories.

The reason is only because there is no `repo - read only` access level supported by Github OAuth. (You can read the discussion here https://github.com/orgs/community/discussions/7891 )

Even though access is requested for read and write, the extension only uses it for read operations, as you can see in the source code.

## Setup for Private Repos owned by an Organization

Access to private repositories owned by an organization is restricted by default. To access the commits graph for such repositories, you need to follow the following steps.

  1. Go to https://github.com/settings/tokens
  2. Create a Personal Access Token (PAT) with the following scopes -
     * repo | Full control of private repositories

> For a more secure option, use a Fine-Grained token (beta) with the following scopes -
> 
>   * repo | Read access to code, commit statuses, and metadata

  3. Go back to the commits tab of a repo owned by the organization.
  4. From the dropdown for "Authorize with GitHub", select "Custom Personal Access Token".
  5. Enter the PAT and click on "Add PAT".

(Full access to repo is required to fetch the commits graph, because there is no read only access level for GitHub OAuth scopes as of now.)

## Tech Stack

Client: JavaScript, Manifest V3

Server: GitHub GraphQL, GitHub OAuth, FireBase Cloud Functions

## Features

  * Authentication with GitHub OAuth ✓
  * Connection to GitHub GraphQL ✓
  * Fetch the commits data from API ✓
  * Fetch further commits on demand ✓
  * Option to specify access level (public only or private too) ✓
  * Hover on the commit dot to see details ✓
  * Option to add custom PAT ✓
  * Filter the commits based on branch ✓

## Contact

Feel free to drop a mail at scaria@scaria.dev or nirmalscaria1@gmail.com

## macOS protected folders (Desktop, Documents)

macOS TCC (Transparency, Consent, and Control) protects certain folders at the kernel level. Without Full Disk Access, Copilot CLI cannot reach `~/Desktop` or `~/Documents` with or without cplt. That is a macOS restriction, not a sandbox limitation, and the cplt sandbox stays fully active either way.

Path  | Without FDA  | With FDA  | Notes
--- | --- | --- | ---
`~/Desktop`  | ❌  | ✅  | TCC-protected
`~/Documents`  | ❌  | ✅  | TCC-protected
`~/Downloads`  | ✅  | ✅  | Less restrictive TCC policy
Dragged screenshots  | ❌  | ✅  | `TemporaryItems/NSIRD_*` are per-process isolated

Fix: grant Full Disk Access to your terminal (recommended):

  1. Open System Settings → Privacy & Security → Full Disk Access
  2. Enable your terminal app (Terminal.app, iTerm2, Ghostty, etc.)
  3. Restart the terminal. TCC grants only take effect for new processes

This lifts TCC restrictions for all child processes, while the cplt sandbox keeps enforcing its own deny-by-default rules (write protection, network filtering, dotfile access, etc.).

## Cloud credential directories

The following directories are entirely blocked, with no read, write, or execute:

Directory  | Purpose
--- | ---
`~/.config/gcloud`  | Google Cloud SDK config, ADC credentials, Python virtualenv
`~/.aws`  | AWS credentials and config
`~/.azure`  | Azure CLI credentials
`~/.kube`  | Kubernetes cluster credentials
`~/.config/op`  | 1Password CLI sessions

### Reading individual files (e.g. Application Default Credentials)

You can grant read-only access to specific files inside these directories with `allow.read`:
    
    # Per session
    cplt --allow-read ~/.config/gcloud/application_default_credentials.json -- -p "deploy"
    
    # Per repo (.cplt.toml)
    cplt config set --repo allow.read ~/.config/gcloud/application_default_credentials.json

This lets GCP SDKs authenticate using the ADC JSON file without exposing the entire directory.

A grant may also name a subdirectory — `~/.aws/sso/cache`, `~/.kube/cache` — and it grants that subtree. It used to grant the subtree on Linux and only the directory entry itself on macOS, where the re-allow was emitted as an SBPL `literal`; the files underneath stayed denied and nothing said so. Linux's reading is now authoritative on both: the grant covers what the user named, and nothing else in the credential directory.

### Executing cloud CLIs (gcloud, aws, az) is blocked by default

Neither the default sandbox nor `allow.read` lets the agent execute binaries inside these directories. `gcloud`, for instance, uses a Python virtualenv at `~/.config/gcloud/virtenv/` that needs execute permission the sandbox does not grant.

This is intentional. Cloud CLIs have unrestricted access to your cloud infrastructure. An agent running `gcloud` could create or delete resources, read secrets, or modify IAM policies. The sandbox closes that escalation path.

Workarounds:

Need  | Solution
--- | ---
GCP authentication for SDKs  | `allow.read ~/.config/gcloud/application_default_credentials.json`, SDKs read the JSON directly
AWS authentication for SDKs  | `allow.read ~/.aws/credentials`, SDKs read credentials directly
Running cloud CLI commands  | Run them outside the sandbox in a regular terminal
CI/CD with cloud access  | Use project-level service account keys or workload identity, not user credentials

> Design principle: `allow.read` grants read access to credential paths so SDKs can authenticate. It does not grant execute permission, because executing cloud CLIs would bypass the sandbox's network and filesystem restrictions.

`allow.exec` is the deliberate opt-out, and it is the only one. It names a path inside a credential directory and grants read plus execute on it — `~/.docker/cli-plugins` and `~/.terraform.d/plugins` are the cases that motivated it. It was honoured on Linux and silently dropped on macOS, where it was emitted before the blanket deny and lost to it; it is now honoured on both. The tree stays read-only either way: the exec-grant write deny is the last rule in the profile, and `sandbox::prepare` refuses an exec grant that overlaps any writable tree.
